blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Who this is for.** A Java full stack developer who must explain, and diagnose, what the operating system does beneath a running service: process and thread management, memory, files, I/O, containers and synchronisation.
- **Every chapter follows the same steps:** (1) the concept and the problem it solves, (2) the mechanism, shown with diagrams, (3) a worked trace or calculation, (4) a hands-on experiment with real commands, C or Java code, (5) **real-world incidents**, each presented as symptoms, diagnosis, root cause, fix and prevention, and (6) the questions interviewers ask, with answers.
- **How to study.** Read each diagram before the prose and narrate it aloud. Reproduce every experiment on a Linux machine or virtual machine (never on a production host). Treat each incident as an exercise: cover the diagnosis, decide which command to run first, then compare with the text.
- **Running the code.** Save a Java listing as `Main.java` and run `java Main.java`; compile C with `gcc -O0 -o demo` `demo.c`. Terminal sessions begin with `$`. Output shown was produced on the build machine unless labelled typical.
- **Scope.** The focus is Linux, the platform on which most Java services run, together with the JVM and container behaviour that interacts with it. Windows and macOS are mentioned only where the difference matters.

sections.title: Version Control and How Git Stores Data

blocks.text:
A backend service is changed by many people, over many months, in many places at once. Without a record of what changed, who changed it and why, three problems appear quickly. A defect introduced last week cannot be located. Two developers editing the same file overwrite each other. A release that worked in production cannot be reproduced, because nobody knows which exact files produced it. A **version control system** (VCS) solves these problems by recording every change to a set of files as an ordered, attributable history, and by providing tools to combine work done in parallel.

Version control systems fall into three generations. *Local* systems (for example RCS) keep a history of single files on one machine. *Centralised* systems (CVS, Subversion) keep one authoritative server; clients hold only the files of one revision, so history operations need the network. *Distributed* systems (Git, Mercurial) give every clone the complete history; commits, branches and log queries run locally, and a server is only a convenient meeting point. Git was written by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for the Linux kernel, and it is the de facto standard for Java and Spring Boot projects, which is why the remaining chapters of this guide (Docker, pipelines, Kubernetes, AWS) all assume a Git repository as the starting point.

This chapter explains the data model. Almost every confusing Git behaviour (why a branch is cheap, why a commit id changes after a rebase, why a deleted commit can still be recovered, why a committed password cannot be unpublished) follows from five facts about how Git stores data. All examples use the small `orders-service` application (Spring Boot 3, Java 21, Maven) that runs through the whole guide. Every command and every output block in this chapter was produced by Git 2.43 on the build machine; commit ids differ on other machines because ids depend on author name and timestamp.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Snapshots, not differences

Many older systems store each revision as a delta against the previous one. Git conceptually stores a **snapshot** of the complete project tree for every commit. Files that did not change are not copied again: the snapshot simply points to the same stored content as the previous one. The result is that reading any revision needs one lookup, not a replay of deltas, and that creating a branch or comparing two revisions is inexpensive.

blocks.text:
Git does apply delta compression, but only as a storage optimisation inside *packfiles* (described later in this chapter). The logical model stays snapshot based.

#### The four object types

Git is a **content-addressable object store**: a key-value database in which the key is the SHA-1 hash of the value. Four kinds of object exist.

rows: The bytes of one file; no name, no permissions
A directory listing: mode, type, id and name of each entry
the root of a commit, or `src/`
One tree id, zero or more parent commit ids, author, committer, message
An annotated tag: target object id, tagger, message
blocks.caption: The four Git object types.

blocks.text:
A blob stores only content. The file name lives in the tree that contains the blob, so two files with identical content, in the same or different directories, share one blob. A commit stores a pointer to the root tree, which records the whole project at that moment, and pointers to its parent commits, which form the history graph.

The object id is computed as the SHA-1 of a header followed by the content: the type, a space, the content length in bytes, a NUL byte, and then the content. Because the id is derived from the content, identical content always yields an identical id, and any change to the content yields a different id. A commit id covers the tree id and the parent ids, so it transitively covers the entire history behind it; this is why altering any old commit changes the id of every later commit.

blocks.text:
SHA-1 is no longer collision resistant against deliberate attack. Git has used a hardened SHA-1 implementation that detects known collision patterns since version 2.13, and it also supports repositories that use SHA-256 (`git init` `--object-format=sha256`), although hosting services do not accept SHA-256 repositories in general and this guide does not use them. The ids in this guide are therefore SHA-1 ids of 40 hexadecimal digits, normally abbreviated to seven.

#### Three areas: working tree, index, repository

Git distinguishes three places where file content lives. The **working tree** holds the files that are edited. The **index**, also called the **staging area** (a binary file, `.git/index`), holds the exact snapshot that the next commit will record. The **repository** (`.git/objects` and `.git/refs`) holds all committed history. `git add` copies content from the working tree into the index; `git commit` turns the index into a tree, wraps it in a commit object and advances the current branch. The staging area makes it possible to commit a selected part of the current work instead of everything.

**git diff git diff --staged**

**git add git commit**

**Working tree Index (staging area) Repository** **files on disk .git/index .git/objects and refs**

**git restore git restore --staged**

**git switch / git checkout (updates index and working tree)**

*git status compares all three areas and reports the differences*

*git commit -a stages tracked modified files first, then commits*

*Figure 1.3. Observe which command moves content between which pair of areas, and which areas the two forms of* `git diff` *compare.*

#### References, branches, tags and HEAD

Objects are immutable and addressed by hash; humans need movable names. A **reference** is a small text file that contains an object id. A **branch** is a reference under `refs/heads/`; a **lightweight tag** is a reference under `refs/tags/` that names a commit directly; an **annotated tag** is a reference to a tag object, which in turn names a commit and carries a message and tagger. **HEAD** is a special reference that normally contains the name of the current branch (`ref: refs/heads/main`). When a commit is created, Git writes the new commit id into the file of the branch that HEAD names. A branch is therefore a 41-byte file (40 digits and a newline), which explains why creating one is instantaneous and why deleting one does not delete commits.

blocks.text:
If HEAD contains a commit id instead of a branch name, the repository is in the **detached HEAD** state. New commits are then reachable only through HEAD and are easy to lose; a later chapter shows how to recover them.

#### Loose objects and packfiles

A newly created object is stored as one zlib-compressed file under `.git/objects/xx/yyyy...`, where `xx` are the first two hexadecimal digits of the id. This is a **loose object**. When the number of loose objects grows, or when `git gc` or a network transfer runs, Git collects objects into a **packfile** (`.git/objects/pack/*.pack` with an index `*.idx`). Inside a pack, similar objects (typically successive versions of the same file) are stored as a full base object plus **deltas**. Network transfer uses the same format, which is why `git clone` of a long history is much smaller than the sum of its snapshots.

**Before git gc: loose objects After git gc: one packfile**

**pack-1ba1155...pack (+ .idx)**

xx/yyyy... xx/yyyy... xx/yyyy... **gc** 9dc7f6e d31529c data.txt, newest older data.txt 18901 B -\> 4520 B delta: 14 B -\> 26 B xx/yyyy... xx/yyyy... xx/yyyy... *delta base (depth 1)* *19 files under .git/objects/xx/* *each zlib-compressed on its own 16 objects stored whole,* *3 as deltas (chain length 1)*

*loose count: 19 -\> 0*

*the snapshot model is logical; the pack is a storage optimisation underneath it*

*Figure 1.5. Observe that after* `git gc` *the nineteen loose files become one pack, and that the older version of* `data.txt` *is stored as a* *14-byte delta against the newest version.*

#### The .git directory

rows: Current branch (`ref: refs/heads/main`) or a commit id when detached
Repository-local configuration: remotes, tracking branches, user name
The object database: loose objects and `pack/`
Packed copy of references, created by `git gc` or `git pack-refs`
The reflog: a history of where HEAD and each branch pointed
Scripts that Git runs at defined events

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### Creating the first commit

The following session creates the repository, adds a README and one Java class, and commits. The `git status` output before the commit lists both paths as untracked.

blocks.code:
$ git -c init.defaultBranch=main init orders-service
Initialized empty Git repository in /tmp/dvw_v1/orders-service/.git/
$ cd orders-service
$ git config user.name "Maruthi Sreeram"
$ git config user.email dev@example.com
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        README.md
        src/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
$ git add README.md src
$ git status --short
A  README.md
A  src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrdersApplication.java
$ git commit -m "Add skeleton of orders-service"
[main (root-commit) 5ef5f11] Add skeleton of orders-service
 2 files changed, 8 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
 create mode 100644 src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrdersApplication.java
blocks.title: Initial repository and first commit

blocks.text:
The `-c init.defaultBranch=main` option names the first branch explicitly, because the built-in default of Git 2.43 is still `master` unless configured. The two `git config` commands store the author identity in `.git/config` of this repository only; the global configuration is not touched.

#### Inspecting the commit and its tree

`git cat-file` reads any object. `-t` prints the type and `-p` pretty-prints the content.

blocks.code:
$ git cat-file -t HEAD
commit
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree bd161700aced243b7f8128fa68b7883003d79ae1
author Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com> 1790829000 +0530
committer Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com> 1790829000 +0530

Add skeleton of orders-service
$ git cat-file -p bd161700aced243b7f8128fa68b7883003d79ae1
100644 blob c0ede6a4cc215d1d2e155b8eaa3f321b9d482618    README.md
040000 tree 039df06ecbfc849bb6dfc9b31cfcfed9f78fefd7    src
$ git ls-tree -r --abbrev HEAD
100644 blob c0ede6a     README.md
100644 blob 1002d27     src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrdersApplication.java
blocks.title: A commit object and the tree it points to

blocks.text:
The first commit has no `parent` line (it is a *root commit*). The numbers `1790829000 +0530` are a Unix timestamp and a time zone offset. `git ls-tree -r` expands all nested trees into a flat list. The mode `100644` marks a regular file, `100755` an executable file, `040000` a directory and `120000` a symbolic link.

#### Verifying the content-addressing rule

The claim that the id is the SHA-1 of a header plus the content can be checked without Git: the README contains 17 bytes, so the hashed text is `blob 17`, a NUL byte, and the content.

blocks.code:
$ git cat-file -t c0ede6a
blob
$ git cat-file -s c0ede6a
17
$ git cat-file -p c0ede6a
# orders-service
$ printf '# orders-service\n' | git hash-object --stdin
c0ede6a4cc215d1d2e155b8eaa3f321b9d482618
$ printf 'blob 17\0# orders-service\n' | sha1sum
c0ede6a4cc215d1d2e155b8eaa3f321b9d482618  -
blocks.title: Reproducing a blob id with sha1sum

blocks.text:
Both commands print the same id. In a SHA-256 repository (`git init --object-format=sha256`) the same input hashes to `dc24a477...469e` with `sha256sum`, which confirms that only the hash function differs.

#### Counting objects

blocks.code:
$ git count-objects -v | head -2
count: 10
size: 40
$ cat .git/refs/heads/main
5ef5f11fdb8c67183b097cd35252f772dc254afa
blocks.title: The object database after one commit

blocks.text:
Ten objects exist: two blobs (the README and the Java file), seven trees (the root, `src`, `main`, `java`, `com`, `example` and `orders`, one per directory level) and one commit. A tree object exists for every directory level, so a deep Maven package layout produces many small trees. The branch file holds exactly the commit id printed by `git commit`.

#### Sharing, and snapshots that cost almost nothing

The second commit adds `pom.xml` and a copy of the README named `COPY.md`. The identical content must not create a new blob.

blocks.code:
$ git add -A && git commit -m "Add pom.xml and a copy of the README"
$ git ls-tree HEAD
100644 blob c0ede6a4cc215d1d2e155b8eaa3f321b9d482618    COPY.md
100644 blob c0ede6a4cc215d1d2e155b8eaa3f321b9d482618    README.md
100644 blob f6afab48ee5fc61a7400934e1749ec33c1ff6952    pom.xml
040000 tree 039df06ecbfc849bb6dfc9b31cfcfed9f78fefd7    src
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 7b20c9265978f2b5a9765ff44f9916b9f2f54430
parent 5ef5f11fdb8c67183b097cd35252f772dc254afa
author Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com> 1790829060 +0530
committer Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com> 1790829060 +0530

Add pom.xml and a copy of the README
blocks.title: Second commit: shared blob and unchanged subtree

blocks.text:
`COPY.md` and `README.md` have the same blob id, and the `src` tree id `039df06` is unchanged, so the second snapshot added only one blob (`pom.xml`), one root tree and one commit. The new commit records `parent 5ef5f11`, which is the link that forms the history.

#### Packfiles and delta compression

To see delta compression, the next two commits add a 2000-line text file and then change a single line in it. Each full version is about 18.9 KB, but the object database is small after `git gc`.

blocks.code:
$ git count-objects -v | egrep 'count|size:|in-pack|packs'
count: 19
size: 84
in-pack: 0
packs: 0
$ git gc -q
$ git count-objects -v | egrep 'count|size:|in-pack|packs'
count: 0
size: 0
in-pack: 19
packs: 1
$ ls .git/objects/pack
pack-1ba1155d7922ffebb22efc79139c306a6ce4618c.idx
pack-1ba1155d7922ffebb22efc79139c306a6ce4618c.pack
pack-1ba1155d7922ffebb22efc79139c306a6ce4618c.rev
$ git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/*.idx | grep blob | sed -E 's/([0-9a-f]{7})[0-9a-f]{33}/\1/g'
c0ede6a blob   17 27 661
9dc7f6e blob   18901 4520 688
f6afab4 blob   169 126 5208
1002d27 blob   161 135 5334
d31529c blob   14 26 5927 1 9dc7f6e
blocks.title: Loose objects, then a packfile

blocks.text:
The columns of `verify-pack -v` are id, type, size, size in the pack and offset; delta objects add the delta depth and the base object. The newest `data.txt` (`9dc7f6e`, 18901 bytes) is stored whole, compressed to 4520 bytes. The previous version (`d31529c`) is stored as a delta of 14 bytes against it, occupying 26 bytes in the pack at depth 1. The nineteen loose files became one pack of three files; the `.rev` file is an auxiliary reverse index written by recent Git versions. The `sed` filter only shortens the ids to seven digits for the page.

The same session also shows why `git gc` seldom needs to be run manually: Git runs `git gc --auto` after commands such as `git commit`, `git merge` and `git fetch` when the loose-object count passes a threshold (the default of `gc.auto` is 6700, from memory; verify with the Git documentation).

#### Annotated and lightweight tags

blocks.code:
$ git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "First tagged build"
$ git cat-file -t v0.1.0
tag
$ git cat-file -p v0.1.0
object d455cf4bd82854380505466ed39a5411961eb506
type commit
tag v0.1.0
tagger Maruthi Sreeram <dev@example.com> 1790829240 +0530

First tagged build
$ git rev-parse v0.1.0 v0.1.0^{commit}
82ec8bf7a8fa42fef738a5218f41a85c952e0772
d455cf4bd82854380505466ed39a5411961eb506
$ git tag light-example && git cat-file -t light-example
commit
$ git symbolic-ref HEAD
refs/heads/main
blocks.title: An annotated tag is its own object

blocks.text:
`v0.1.0` resolves to the tag object `82ec8bf`; the suffix `^{commit}` peels it to the commit. A lightweight tag (`light-example`) is a plain reference whose type is `commit`. Annotated tags are the correct choice for releases, because they record who tagged, when, and why, and because tools such as `git describe` and GitHub Releases rely on them.

### Hands-on

Work in an empty directory and write each prediction before running the command.

1. Run `git init`, create `A.txt` containing `hello`, then `git add A.txt` and `git commit -m one`. Predict the `count` line of `git count-objects -v` (one blob, one tree, one commit: `count: 3`).
2. Create `B.txt` with the same content and commit it. The count grows by two (a new tree and a new commit; the blob is reused), giving `count: 5`; `git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}` shows one blob id for both names. Verify the id by hand: `printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha1sum` equals `git hash-object A.txt`.
3. Compare `cat .git/refs/heads/main` with `git rev-parse HEAD`, run `git gc`, and compare `git count-objects -v` before and after.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: the repository is 300 MB although the source is tiny

**Scenario.** A new team member clones `orders-service` and the clone takes minutes and occupies hundreds of megabytes, although the Java sources total a few hundred kilobytes.

**Symptoms.** `git clone` transfers a large pack; `du -sh .git` is far larger than the working tree.

**Diagnosis.** `git count-objects -vH` shows the size of the object database. Listing the largest blobs reveals the cause:

blocks.code:
$ git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectsize) %(rest)' \
    | grep '^blob' | sort -k2 -n -r | head -3
blob 5000000 orders-service.jar
blob 11 A.java
blocks.title: Finding the largest objects in the history

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** A build artifact (`target/`, a fat jar, a database dump) was committed once. Git stores every version of every file ever committed, so deleting the file in a later commit does not shrink the history. A random 5 MB file named `orders-service.jar` was committed in a test repository for this guide and removed in the next commit; `git` `count-objects -vH` still reported `size: 4.80 MiB` afterwards, and the listing above shows the blob.

**Fix.** Remove the file from all history with a history rewrite (`git filter-repo --invert-paths --path target/` or, if that tool is unavailable, `git filter-branch`), expire the reflog and run `git gc --prune=now`. The procedure and its measured effect are shown in the chapter on recovering from mistakes. Every collaborator must then re-clone or rebase.

**Prevention.** Add `target/` and `*.jar` to `.gitignore` in the first commit; keep binaries in an artifact repository (Maven repository, container registry) and large assets in Git LFS.

#### Problem: an empty directory is missing after clone

**Scenario.** The application expects a `logs/` directory that exists on the developer's machine and is absent after a fresh clone.

**Symptoms.** `git status` ignores the empty directory.

**Diagnosis.** Git tracks blobs; a tree entry exists only for directories that contain at least one tracked file.

**Root cause.** The data model has no object for an empty directory.

**Fix.** Add a placeholder file, by convention `.gitkeep` (measured: after `touch logs/.gitkeep`, `git status --short` printed `?? logs/` and `git ls-tree -r HEAD` listed `logs/.gitkeep` with the empty-blob id `e69de29`).

**Prevention.** Create required directories in application start-up code or in the Dockerfile.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the distributed version control system: a command-line tool and a data format. GitHub is a hosting service that stores Git repositories and adds pull requests, issues, access control and automation (Actions). Alternatives with the same relationship to Git are GitLab and Bitbucket. A repository works without any host.

#### Does Git store differences or snapshots?

Logically, every commit refers to a complete snapshot (a root tree). Unchanged files are shared between snapshots through identical blob ids. Physically, packfiles apply delta compression between similar objects, but that is an internal optimisation.

#### What are the four Git object types?

Blob (file content), tree (directory listing), commit (root tree, parents, author, message) and tag (annotated tag object). All are identified by the SHA-1 of their header and content.

#### What is a branch, technically?

A file under `.git/refs/heads/` that contains one commit id. Committing moves the file's value forward; creating or deleting a branch never copies or removes commits.

#### How is a commit id computed, and why does rebasing change it?

It is the SHA-1 of the commit text: tree id, parent ids, author and committer with timestamps, and the message. A rebase changes the parent, so the id changes, together with the ids of all descendants.

#### What are HEAD and the index?

HEAD is a reference to the current branch (or directly to a commit when detached). The index is the staging area: the proposed content of the next commit.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "A file was deleted in the latest commit. Is it still in the repository?" Yes. The latest tree no longer lists it, but every earlier commit still references its blob, so it remains in the object database and is retrievable with `git show <commit>:path`. Only a history rewrite followed by expiring the reflog and garbage collection removes it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Git stores a snapshot (a root tree) per commit; unchanged files are shared through identical blob ids.

- Four object types: blob, tree, commit, tag; each id is the SHA-1 of `type size NUL content`.
- A branch is a file containing a commit id; HEAD usually names a branch; tags point to commits.
- The working tree, the index and the repository are three separate areas; `git add` and `git commit` move content between them.
- `git gc` packs loose objects and delta-compresses similar versions; history is never shrunk by deleting a file in a later commit.

Daily work with Git is a loop of a few commands: inspect, stage, commit, share. The loop is simple, but each command has options that prevent mistakes (staging parts of a file, undoing safely, finding the commit that broke a test). This chapter covers the commands used several times a day, the three forms of `git reset` that cause most data-loss accidents, and two diagnostic tools, `git bisect` and `git blame`, that are valuable in a team. The examples extend the `orders-service` repository from the previous chapter.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The state of a file

At any moment a file is *untracked* (unknown to Git), *unmodified*, *modified* in the working tree, or *staged* in the index. `git status` reports the combination; in the short format (`--short`) the first column shows the index state relative to HEAD and the second column the working tree state relative to the index. `M` means staged modification, `M` unstaged modification, `MM` both (a file staged and then edited again), `A` newly added, `??` untracked and `UU` unmerged (conflict).

#### Commits as units of change

A commit should contain one logical change, build on its own, and carry a message that states what and why. The conventional layout is a subject line of at most about 50 to 72 characters in the imperative mood ("Add discount calculation"), a blank line, and an optional body that explains the reasoning. Small, coherent commits make `git` `bisect`, `git revert` and code review practical. Conventions that standardise the subject line (Conventional Commits) are covered in the chapter on team workflows.

#### .gitignore

A `.gitignore` file lists patterns of files that Git must not track or show as untracked. It affects only untracked files: a file that is already tracked stays tracked until removed from the index. Patterns support `*` wildcards, a trailing `/` for directories, `!` for negation, and `**` for any number of directories. For a Maven project in IntelliJ IDEA the typical content is shown below; `.env` and `application-local.properties` are included because local files often hold passwords.

**.gitignore**

blocks.code:
# Maven build output
target/
# IntelliJ IDEA
.idea/
*.iml
out/
# Eclipse / VS Code
.classpath
.project
.settings/
.vscode/
# OS files
.DS_Store
# Local configuration that may contain secrets
application-local.properties
.env

blocks.text:
The editor-specific and operating-system-specific entries can alternatively be placed in a user-level file configured with `git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global`, so that the project file lists only project concerns.

#### The three forms of reset

`git reset` moves the current branch to another commit and optionally updates the index and the working tree to match. The mode decides how far the change reaches.

blocks.caption: What git reset --mode HEAD~2 changes.

blocks.text:
**after reset HEAD~2 main, HEAD (before)**

`C1 C2 C3` *reset HEAD~2 moves the branch* *back to C1; C2 and C3 stay in* *the object database (reflog)*

**git reset --soft git reset --mixed (default) git reset --hard**

**Branch / HEAD** moved to C1 moved to C1 moved to C1

kept: still holds reset to C1 **Index (staged)** reset to C1 C3 + staged edits (edits unstaged)

kept: edits stay overwritten: **Working tree** kept on disk uncommitted work lost

*soft: undo the commits only. mixed: also unstage. hard: also discard working-tree edits.* *only --hard can destroy uncommitted work; committed work stays recoverable through the reflog*

*Figure 1.6. Observe that all three modes move the branch, that only* `--mixed` *and* `--hard` *touch the index, and that only* `--hard` *overwrites the working tree and therefore destroys uncommitted edits.*

`git revert` is the safe counterpart for commits that have already been shared: it creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier one and leaves history intact.

blocks.text:
#### Finding a defect with bisect and blame

`git bisect` performs a binary search through history. The developer names one commit known to be good and one known to be bad; Git checks out the middle commit, a test decides, and the range halves until the first bad commit is found. For N candidate commits, about log2(N) tests are needed, so a range of 1000 commits needs about ten. `git` `bisect run <command>` automates the test: exit status 0 means good, 1 to 127 except 125 means bad, 125 means "cannot test this commit, skip it", and 128 or higher aborts the bisection.

blocks.text:
`git blame` shows, for each line of a file, the commit and author that last changed it. It identifies who to ask and which commit explains a line; it is not a tool for assigning fault.

### Worked example

#### Ignoring build output

The working tree contains build output and IDE files next to source files. Before a `.gitignore` exists they all appear as untracked; after creating it they disappear, and `git check-ignore -v` names the rule that matched.

blocks.code:
$ git status --short
?? .idea/
?? .idea_x
?? orders.iml
?? src/
?? target/
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
?? .idea_x
?? src/
$ git check-ignore -v target/orders-service.jar .idea/workspace.xml
.gitignore:2:target/    target/orders-service.jar
.gitignore:4:.idea/     .idea/workspace.xml
blocks.title: Creating .gitignore and verifying the rules

blocks.text:
The first listing is taken before and the second after the `.gitignore` of the previous section was created. `.idea_x` is an unrelated test file that the rules deliberately do not match. The output of `check-ignore -v` has the form `file:line:pattern` followed by the ignored path.

#### Staging, diffing and committing

blocks.code:
$ git add .gitignore src && git status --short
A  .gitignore
A  src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java
A  src/main/resources/application.properties
$ git diff --staged --stat
 .gitignore                                         | 16 ++++++++++++++++
 src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java |  7 +++++++
 src/main/resources/application.properties          |  3 +++
 3 files changed, 26 insertions(+)
$ git commit -m "Add OrderService and base configuration"
[main (root-commit) 40b94a1] Add OrderService and base configuration
 3 files changed, 26 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java
 create mode 100644 src/main/resources/application.properties
blocks.title: Reviewing changes before they are committed

blocks.text: After a line is appended to `README.md`, `git diff` shows the unstaged change and `git diff --staged` shows what is already staged. The unified diff format marks removed lines with `-`, added lines with `+`, and each hunk starts with `@@` `-old,count +new,count @@`.

blocks.code:
$ git diff
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index c0ede6a..d6fc9c3 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 # orders-service
+Order management API.
blocks.title: An unstaged diff

blocks.text:
The line `index c0ede6a..d6fc9c3` names the blob ids before and after, which are the same ids that `git cat-file` accepts (`c0ede6a` is the README blob from the first chapter section). `git add -p` stages hunk by hunk and is the usual way to split a mixed change into separate commits.

#### Amending the last commit

`git commit --amend --no-edit -m "..."` replaces the most recent commit with a new one; in a test the id changed from `8976e8d` to `f8f58e4` because the message is part of the hashed content. It is appropriate only before the commit is pushed. The `Date:` line that Git printed is an artefact of the fixed author date of the build environment.

#### Reading history

A history of a few commits was built by committing six small changes. The common read-only views follow.

blocks.code:
$ git log --oneline
642ed56 Document discount method
9381d27 Round shipping threshold
c48b294 Update tax rate for new slab
b8a3754 Add shipping fee
fe94f91 Add discount calculation
1a703ba Extract TAX_RATE constant
f8f58e4 Add totalWithTax to OrderService
40b94a1 Add OrderService and base configuration
$ git log --graph --pretty=tformat:"%h %an %ad %s" --date=short -3
* 642ed56 Maruthi Sreeram 2026-10-01 Document discount method
* 9381d27 Maruthi Sreeram 2026-10-01 Round shipping threshold
* c48b294 Maruthi Sreeram 2026-10-01 Update tax rate for new slab
$ git log -S"TAX_RATE" --oneline
1a703ba Extract TAX_RATE constant
blocks.title: Log formats

blocks.text:
The format placeholders of the second command are `%h` (short id), `%an` (author), `%ad` (date) and `%s` (subject). `git log` `-S"text"` (the "pickaxe") lists the commits that changed the number of occurrences of the text, which locates the commit that introduced or removed a symbol. Other frequently used filters are `--author`, `--since`, `--grep` and a path after `--`.

#### Reset, compared in practice

Three experimental commits are made on a scratch branch, followed by one staged edit and one unstaged edit, so that `git status --short` prints `MM` (staged and unstaged changes in one file). Each experiment restarts from that state and runs `git reset --<mode> HEAD~2`; the last lines of the file show which edits survive.

blocks.title: git reset --soft HEAD~2

blocks.code:
$ git reset --mixed HEAD~2
Unstaged changes after reset:
M       src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java
$ git status --short
 M src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java
blocks.title: git reset --mixed HEAD~2
git reset --hard HEAD~2

blocks.text:
With `--soft` the two commits are undone but the staged and the unstaged edits survive, so one fresh `git commit` can combine the work of the undone commits (the basis of "squash the last N commits"). With `--mixed` the index is also reset, so everything becomes an unstaged modification (the file content is the same as in the soft case). With `--hard` the file returns to the content of `Experiment 1`: `change 2`, `change 3`, the staged edit and the unstaged edit are gone from the working tree. The committed lines remain recoverable through the reflog (see the chapter on recovering from mistakes); the uncommitted ones do not.

#### Restore, revert and stash

`git restore <path>` discards unstaged edits of a file by copying it from the index; `git restore --staged <path>` unstages it and keeps the edit. Both were introduced in Git 2.23 to replace the overloaded `git checkout -- <path>` and `git reset HEAD <path>`. `git revert --no-edit HEAD` creates a commit with the message `Revert "..."` that undoes an earlier one (shown in the chapter on recovering from mistakes). `git stash push -u -m "wip"` parks tracked and untracked changes so that the working tree is clean for an urgent task:

blocks.code:
$ git stash push -u -m "wip: shipping notes"
Saved working directory and index state On main: wip: shipping notes
$ git stash list
stash@{0}: On main: wip: shipping notes
$ git stash pop
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (0115a337006028982f22afc9863964d1e77341e5)
blocks.title: Parking and restoring work

blocks.text:
`git stash pop` reapplies the newest stash and drops it (the lines that list the restored files are omitted here); `git` `stash apply` reapplies and keeps it. A stash is stored as commit objects under `refs/stash`.

#### Bisect, with a real automated test

The history above contains a defect: after the commit "Update tax rate for new slab" the constant `TAX_RATE` is `0.81` instead of `0.18`, so `totalWithTax(100, 1)` returns 181.0 instead of 118.0. The test script `check_tax.sh` (kept outside the repository) compiles `OrderService.java` with `javac`, calls the method and exits with status 0 when the result is 118.0 and 1 otherwise.

blocks.text: Three test runs identified the commit among eight. `git bisect reset` is mandatory afterwards: it returns to the original branch. The session also compiled the Java source on every step, so the script could equally call `mvn -q test` `-Dtest=OrderServiceTest` for a real project. `git blame` on the same line names the commit directly when the cause is a single line:

blocks.code:
$ git blame -L 4,4 --date=short -- src/main/java/com/example/orders/OrderService.java

blocks.title: Blame on a single line

blocks.text:
#### Tags and releases

`git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"` creates an annotated tag; `git describe` names the current commit relative to the nearest tag, for example `v1.0.0-3-g5725d1f` when three commits follow it, which is useful for version strings of snapshot builds. Tags are not pushed by `git push` unless named (`git push origin v1.0.0`).

### Hands-on

1. Create a repository with three commits, each appending one line to `notes.txt` (`one`, `two`, `three`). Append `four` and stage it, then append `five` without staging. `git status --short` must print `MM notes.txt`.
2. Run `git branch backup`, then `git reset --soft HEAD~2`; inspect `git status` and `git log --oneline`; return with `git reset --hard backup`. Repeat with `--mixed` and `--hard`; after `--hard`, `notes.txt` lacks `four` and `five`.
3. Write `check.sh` (kept outside the working tree) that exits 1 when `notes.txt` contains `two`, and run `git bisect` `start HEAD <first-commit>` followed by `git bisect run ../check.sh` to find the commit that introduced the line; finish with `git bisect reset`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a commit was made on the wrong branch

**Scenario.** A developer commits a coupon-validation change on `main` instead of on the feature branch `feature/coupons`.

**Symptoms.** `git log` on `main` shows an unwanted commit; the feature branch lacks it. Nothing has been pushed yet.

**Diagnosis.** `git log --oneline --decorate --all --graph` shows which branch pointers are where.

blocks.code:
$ git log --oneline --decorate --all --graph
* a9092e1 (HEAD -> main) Add coupon validation (committed on main by mistake)
* 7adb1c0 (feature/coupons) Initial
blocks.title: The commit is on main; the feature branch is one commit behind

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** The branch was not switched before committing. A branch is only a pointer; the commit itself is correct.

**Fix.** Copy the commit to the correct branch, then move `main` back. (If the commit message is the only problem, `git` `branch feature/coupons` followed by the reset below is equivalent.)

blocks.code:
$ git switch feature/coupons
Switched to branch 'feature/coupons'
$ git cherry-pick main
[feature/coupons a9092e1] Add coupon validation (committed on main by mistake)
 Date: Thu Oct 1 10:02:00 2026 +0530
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 B.java
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
HEAD is now at 7adb1c0 Initial
$ git log --oneline --decorate --all --graph
* a9092e1 (feature/coupons) Add coupon validation (committed on main by mistake)
* 7adb1c0 (HEAD -> main) Initial
blocks.title: Move the commit to the feature branch and rewind main

blocks.text:
The cherry-picked commit has the same id here only because the parent, timestamps and content are identical in this reproducible test; in ordinary use the copy has a new id. If the changes were not yet committed, `git switch -c` `feature/audit` carries uncommitted edits to the new branch without further steps (measured: `git status --short` printed `?? C.java` after the switch). **Prevention.** Show the current branch in the shell prompt, and protect `main` with a branch protection rule so that direct commits cannot be pushed (see the chapter on GitHub).

#### Problem: a file is still tracked after it was added to .gitignore

**Scenario.** `target/app.jar` was committed by mistake; later `target/` was added to `.gitignore`, but the jar still appears as modified after every build.

**Symptoms.** `git status` lists `M target/app.jar` although the path is ignored.

**Diagnosis.** `git ls-files target` lists the file, which proves that it is in the index.

**Root cause.** `.gitignore` applies only to untracked files.

**Fix.** Remove the file from the index but keep it on disk, then commit:

blocks.code:
$ git status --short
 M target/app.jar
?? .gitignore
$ git rm -r --cached target -q; git status --short
D  target/app.jar
?? .gitignore
blocks.title: Untracking without deleting

blocks.text:
The staged deletion removes the file from future snapshots only; earlier commits still contain it (see the chapter on recovering from mistakes for history cleaning). **Prevention.** Create `.gitignore` before the first `git add -A`.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between `git reset --soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard`?

All three move the current branch to the target commit. `--soft` leaves the index and the working tree unchanged; `--mixed` (the default) also resets the index, so changes remain as unstaged edits; `--hard` resets the index and overwrites the working tree, which discards uncommitted work.

#### When is `git revert` preferable to `git reset`?

When the commit has been pushed or shared. Revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so history is only appended and teammates need no special action. Reset rewrites history and requires a force push.

#### What does `git commit --amend` do, and when is it unsafe?

It replaces the last commit with a new one (new id). It is unsafe after the commit has been pushed to a shared branch, because others may have based work on the old commit.

#### How is `git restore` different from `git checkout`?

`git checkout` combined switching branches and restoring files. Since Git 2.23, `git switch` handles branches and `git` `restore` handles files, which separates the two meanings.

#### How does `git bisect` work, and how many steps does it need?

It performs a binary search over the commits between a known good and a known bad commit; the step count is about log2(N). With `git bisect run <script>` the search is automatic and the script's exit code decides good or bad.

#### How can the commit that introduced a string be found?

`git log -S"string"` (pickaxe) lists commits that changed the number of occurrences; `git log -G"regex"` matches added or removed lines; `git blame` shows the last change per line.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The working tree, index and repository are separate; `git status --short` shows the first two columns of that relationship.

- `.gitignore` affects untracked files only; use `git rm --cached` to untrack a file.
- `reset --soft/--mixed/--hard` differ in how far they reach; only `--hard` destroys uncommitted work.
- Use `git revert` for shared history and `git reset` or `--amend` only for local commits.
- `git bisect run` finds the first bad commit in about log2(N) test runs; `git blame` and `git log -S` locate the origin of a line.

Parallel work is the reason a team uses a version control system. One developer builds discount rules while another upgrades a dependency and a third fixes a defect in production. Each needs an isolated line of work that can be combined later, with a clear record of how it was combined. Git provides this through branches, which cost almost nothing, and through two ways of combining them: **merging**, which records a join in the history, and **rebasing**, which rewrites a branch so that it appears to have started from a newer commit. This chapter explains both mechanisms, shows the conflict markers and the resolution procedure produced by real Git runs, and states the rule that keeps rebasing safe.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Branch pointers and HEAD

A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, as described in the data-model chapter. `git switch -c feature/x` creates a pointer at the current commit and moves HEAD to it; each new commit advances only the pointer that HEAD names. Two branches diverge when each has commits that the other lacks. The *merge base* of two branches is their most recent common ancestor, and it is the reference point for every merge.

#### Fast-forward and three-way merge

`git merge feature` combines the history of `feature` into the current branch. If the current branch is an ancestor of `feature`, no real combining is needed: Git moves the branch pointer forward (a **fast-forward**) and creates no commit.

**Before: git merge feature (from main) After: fast-forward**

**main feature main feature**

blocks.code: C1          C2          C3         C4                              C1          C2         C3          C4

blocks.text:
*main is an ancestor of feature, so git only moves the main pointer to C4* *no new commit is created; the history stays a straight line*

*Figure 1.9. Observe that the fast-forward moves only the* `main` *pointer from C2 to C4 and creates no new commit.*

If both branches have new commits, Git performs a **three-way merge** using the two branch tips and their merge base. It creates a **merge commit** with two parents. The option `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward would be possible, which preserves the fact that a group of commits was developed on a branch.

blocks.text:
#### Conflicts

Git combines changes automatically when the two sides changed different regions of a file. When both sides changed the same lines differently, Git cannot decide and stops with a **conflict**: the merge is left half done, the affected files contain conflict markers, and `git status` lists them as *unmerged* (`UU`). The developer edits the files to the intended final content, stages them with `git add`, and completes the merge with `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`). `git` `merge --abort` restores the state before the merge. The marker syntax is shown in the worked example below.

#### Rebase

`git rebase main`, run on a feature branch, finds the commits that exist only on the feature branch, sets them aside, moves the branch to the tip of `main`, and replays the commits one by one. Each replayed commit is a *new* commit: it has the same change and message but a different parent, and therefore a different id.

blocks.text:
#### The golden rule of rebasing

**Never rebase commits that other people may already have based work on.** Rebasing replaces commits; anyone who still has the old ones will see the branch as diverged and, when integrating, may reintroduce the old commits next to the new ones. Rebasing local, unpushed commits, or a feature branch owned by one person, is safe. The corollary is that `git push --force` on a shared branch is dangerous; `--force-with-lease` (explained in the chapter on remotes) narrows the danger but does not remove the rule.

#### Interactive rebase

`git rebase -i <base>` opens a todo list with one line per commit, oldest first. Editing the verb at the start of each line changes the outcome.

rows: Keep the changes, edit the message
Stop after applying the commit so that it can be amended or split
Meld into the previous commit and combine both messages
Meld into the previous commit and discard this message

blocks.text:
`git commit --fixup <id>` creates a commit whose message is prefixed `fixup!`, and `git rebase -i --autosquash` arranges such commits automatically, so corrections can be made when noticed and folded in later.

#### Cherry-pick

`git cherry-pick <commit>` applies the change introduced by one commit onto the current branch as a new commit. It is the standard way to move a single fix, for example a production hotfix, to a release branch.

#### A real conflict in pom.xml

Two branches each add a Maven dependency at the end of the `<dependencies>` section of `pom.xml`: `main` adds `spring-boot-starter-validation`, the branch `feature/actuator` adds `spring-boot-starter-actuator`.

blocks.code:
$ git merge feature/actuator
Auto-merging pom.xml
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in pom.xml
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status --short
UU pom.xml
$ git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U
pom.xml
blocks.title: The merge stops with a conflict

blocks.text:
`UU` means both sides modified the file. The relevant part of `pom.xml` now contains conflict markers.

**pom.xml (conflict region, markers shown literally)**

blocks.code:
<dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
<<<<<<< HEAD
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
=======
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
>>>>>>> feature/actuator
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>

blocks.text:
The block between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is the content of the current branch (`main`); the block between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature/actuator` comes from the branch being merged. Only the single differing line is in conflict, because Git matched the surrounding lines (`<groupId>`, `</dependency>`) as common to both sides.

A resolution that merely deletes the three marker lines and keeps both artifact ids would leave one `<dependency>` element with two `<artifactId>` children. In the test run this variant was parsed by Python's XML parser without complaint, which shows that a syntax check does not detect it; Maven would report or ignore the duplicate. The correct result contains two complete dependencies:

**pom.xml (resolved, end of the file)**

blocks.code:
<dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>

### Hands-on

1. Create a repository with one commit and two branches `a` and `b`. On `a`, change line 1 of a file to `from a`; on `b`, to `from` `b`; commit both. On `a`, run `git merge b`, identify the marker regions, resolve to `from a and b`, `git add`, and `git` `commit --no-edit`. Confirm two parents with `git cat-file -p HEAD`.
2. Undo with `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and repeat with `git rebase b` on `a`. The conflict now appears while replaying a commit; resolve it and run `git rebase --continue`. Compare the two histories with `git log --oneline --graph`.
3. Create four commits named `one`, `wip`, `fix`, `two`; run `git rebase -i HEAD~4`, mark `wip` and `fix` as `fixup`, and verify that two commits remain.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: merge conflict in pom.xml

**Scenario.** Two developers add dependencies to `orders-service` on separate branches. The second merge stops with `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in pom.xml`.

**Symptoms.** `git status` shows `UU pom.xml`; the build fails with an XML or Maven parse error if the file is committed with markers still in it.

**Diagnosis.** `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` lists unmerged files, and `grep -n` `'^<<<<<<<\|^=======\|^>>>>>>>' pom.xml` locates every marker. `git diff` during a conflict shows the combined (three-way) diff. **Root cause.** Both branches edited the same region of the file, here the end of `<dependencies>`. Dependency lists are conflict-prone because new entries are conventionally appended at the same place.

**Fix.** Keep both complete dependencies (see the worked example), remove all markers, run `mvn -q verify`, then `git` `add pom.xml` and `git commit`. If the situation is unclear, `git merge --abort` returns to the state before the merge. Resolving conflicts in an IDE merge tool (IntelliJ IDEA shows three panes) reduces errors.

**Prevention.** Merge or rebase `main` into the feature branch regularly, keep branches short, keep dependency versions in properties or a BOM in an order (alphabetical) that reduces coincident edits, and run the build on the merge result in continuous integration.

#### Problem: a long-lived feature branch drifts away from main

**Scenario.** The branch `feature/shipping` lived for four weeks while `main` received many commits. Merging it now produces dozens of conflicts and test failures that no single commit explains.

**Symptoms.** The pull request shows a huge diff; the branch no longer builds after a merge.

**Diagnosis.** The divergence can be measured. In the test repository, with one commit only on `main` and two only on the feature branch:

blocks.code:
$ git rev-list --left-right --count main...feature/shipping
1       2
$ git log --oneline --left-right main...feature/shipping
> 4566702 Add flat shipping fee
> b22ec32 Add Shipping class
< 5940570 Fix null customer in validator
$ git merge-base main feature/shipping
5725d1f14ee53901c7f7a8ecc5bea385a580582c
blocks.title: Measuring divergence

blocks.text:
The first number is the count of commits only on `main` (`<`), the second the count only on the feature branch (`>`). On a drifted branch the first number is large, and the merge base is old.

**Root cause.** Integration was deferred. The cost of a merge grows faster than the number of commits, because later changes build on assumptions that the branch never saw.

**Fix.** Integrate in steps: `git merge main` (or `git rebase main`) into the branch repeatedly, resolving a small number of conflicts each time, or split the branch into smaller pull requests that can be merged separately. `git rerere` (reuse recorded resolution) remembers conflict resolutions and replays them for repeated rebases.

**Prevention.** Keep branches alive for days, not weeks; merge unfinished but safe work behind a feature flag (see the chapter on branching strategies); rebase or merge `main` at least daily.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between merge and rebase?

Merge joins two histories with a merge commit and preserves the real topology; existing commits stay unchanged. Rebase replays commits on a new base, producing new commits and a linear history; it rewrites history and must not be applied to shared commits.

#### What is a fast-forward merge?

A merge in which the current branch is an ancestor of the merged branch. Git moves the branch pointer forward without creating a merge commit.

#### How is a merge conflict resolved?

Open each file listed as unmerged, choose or combine the content between the markers, remove the markers, build and test, `git add` the file, and finish with `git commit` (merge) or `git rebase --continue` (rebase). `git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` cancels.

#### What does `git rebase -i` allow, and when is it used?

It lets a developer reorder, reword, edit, squash, fixup or drop local commits before sharing them, producing a clean history for review.

#### When is cherry-pick appropriate?

To apply a specific commit, typically a fix, onto another branch such as a release branch, without merging everything else from the source branch.

#### State the golden rule of rebasing and the reason for it.

Do not rebase commits that exist in a shared repository and that others may have based work on. Rebasing creates new commits; colleagues holding the old ones would then have to reconcile two versions of the same work.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A branch is a pointer; merging joins histories, rebasing replays commits as new ones.

- Fast-forward moves a pointer; a three-way merge creates a commit with two parents using the merge base.
- Conflicts occur only when both sides changed the same lines; resolve, build, `git add`, continue.
- Rebase and `--amend` rewrite history: use them on private commits only.
- Interactive rebase (`pick`, `reword`, `squash`, `fixup`, `drop`) cleans a branch before review; cherry-pick copies one commit.

Git rarely destroys committed work, but several commands make it unreachable, and several mistakes (a pushed password, a committed jar) cannot be undone by deleting a file. Recovery depends on two facts from the data-model chapter: objects are immutable and remain in the database until garbage collection, and the **reflog** records where HEAD and each branch pointed in the recent past. This chapter shows the recovery of a deleted branch, of a commit lost to `git reset --hard`, and of work done in a detached HEAD, then the three cases that require more than a pointer move: undoing a commit that was already pushed, removing a file from all history, and handling a leaked secret.

### Concept and mechanism

#### The reflog

Every update of HEAD and of every branch is recorded in `.git/logs`. `git reflog` prints the entries of HEAD, newest first, as `HEAD@{n}`; `git reflog show <branch>` prints those of a branch. The log is local to the repository: it is neither pushed nor cloned. By default, entries that are reachable are kept for 90 days and unreachable ones for 30 days (the settings `gc.reflogExpire` and `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable`; the figures are from memory and should be verified against the Git documentation). After the entry expires, `git gc` may delete the commit objects.

#### Reachability

A commit is *reachable* if it can be found by following parent links from a branch, a tag or another reference. Unreachable objects are not deleted immediately; `git gc` prunes them after a grace period (two weeks by default for loose unreachable objects, from memory). `git fsck --lost-found` lists unreachable commits and other objects ("dangling") even when the reflog has already expired.

#### What cannot be undone by moving pointers

Moving pointers recovers *committed* work in the local repository. It does not recover uncommitted changes destroyed by `git reset --hard` or `git restore`, and it cannot withdraw data already sent to a remote: anyone who cloned, forked or cached the repository holds the objects. Secrets are therefore handled as compromised from the moment of the push.

### Worked example

#### Recovering a deleted branch

Two commits were made on `feature/coupons`, and the branch was deleted with `git branch -D` before it was merged.

blocks.code:
$ git branch -D feature/coupons
Deleted branch feature/coupons (was 7314685).
$ git reflog -8
605cca9 HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from feature/coupons to main
7314685 HEAD@{1}: commit: Extend Coupon
bbc716d HEAD@{2}: commit: Add Coupon
605cca9 HEAD@{3}: checkout: moving from main to feature/coupons
605cca9 HEAD@{4}: commit: Order change 3
3c64ee3 HEAD@{5}: commit: Order change 2
601982d HEAD@{6}: commit (initial): Order change 1
$ git branch feature/coupons-recovered 7314685
$ git log --oneline feature/coupons-recovered -3
7314685 Extend Coupon
bbc716d Add Coupon
605cca9 Order change 3
blocks.title: Deleting and recovering a branch

blocks.text:
`git branch -D` printed the id of the tip (`was 7314685`), which already was the recovery key. In general the reflog entry that precedes the move away from the branch (`HEAD@{1}`) is the last commit that the branch contained.

#### Recovering from git reset --hard

A commit `Add report generator` is created and then discarded by a mistaken `git reset --hard HEAD~1`.

blocks.code:
$ git log --oneline -2
8d32c2d Add report generator
605cca9 Order change 3
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
HEAD is now at 605cca9 Order change 3
$ git reflog -3
605cca9 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
8d32c2d HEAD@{1}: commit: Add report generator
605cca9 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from feature/coupons to main
$ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
HEAD is now at 8d32c2d Add report generator
blocks.title: Undoing a hard reset

blocks.text:
The reset itself is an entry in the reflog (`HEAD@{0}`); `HEAD@{1}` is the state before it. `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` returns to it. `ORIG_HEAD` is a shorthand that Git sets before dangerous operations such as reset, merge and rebase, so `git` `reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` often achieves the same.

#### Recovering work from a detached HEAD

blocks.code:
$ git switch --detach HEAD~2
HEAD is now at 3c64ee3 Order change 2
$ echo "lost?" > Lost.java && git add -A && git commit -m "Commit on detached HEAD"
$ git switch main
Warning: you are leaving 1 commit behind, not connected to
any of your branches:
  77fb72f Commit on detached HEAD
If you want to keep it by creating a new branch, this may be a good time
to do so with:
 git branch <new-branch-name> 77fb72f
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git reflog -4
8d32c2d HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from 77fb72f238c813484ef4cb82e22da3548777ae6b to main
77fb72f HEAD@{1}: commit: Commit on detached HEAD
3c64ee3 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to HEAD~2
8d32c2d HEAD@{3}: reset: moving to HEAD@{1}
$ git branch rescued HEAD@{1}
$ git log --oneline rescued -2
77fb72f Commit on detached HEAD
3c64ee3 Order change 2
blocks.title: Commits made on a detached HEAD

blocks.text:
Git warns when leaving the detached state with unreferenced commits and prints the exact command that saves them. If the warning was missed, the reflog contains the commit. The rule is to create a branch (`git switch -c <name>`) before committing in a detached HEAD, or immediately afterwards.

#### Finding objects when the reflog has no entry

`git fsck --lost-found` lists unreachable ("dangling") commits even after `git reflog expire --expire=now --all`; in a test the dropped commit was still listed (`dangling commit 0ee58ca...`) because garbage collection had not run. A deleted *file* is recovered from an earlier commit with `git restore --source=<commit> -- <path>`.

#### Undoing a commit that is already pushed

For a pushed commit the safe action is `git revert`, which appends an inverse commit and needs no force. The example uses a bare repository `o.git` as the remote.

blocks.code:
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD
[main d5b2831] Revert "b work"
 Date: Thu Oct 1 10:00:00 2026 +0530
 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
 delete mode 100644 b.txt
$ git push
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/d1/o.git
   96aae76..d5b2831  main -> main
blocks.title: Reverting and pushing

blocks.text:
For a merge commit, `git revert -m 1 <merge>` names the parent that stays as the mainline. After reverting a merge, a later re-merge of the same branch brings nothing in unless the revert itself is reverted first; this is a known trap.

#### Removing a committed secret or file from all history

A test repository received four commits: a configuration file, the same file with a password, a 5 MB jar, and a source file. The password and the jar are to be removed from every commit. First, deleting them in a new commit does not help:

blocks.code:
$ git log -p -S"S3cr3t" --oneline -- src/main/resources/application.properties \
    | grep -E "^[0-9a-f]{7} |^[+-]spring.datasource.password"
506ebf6 Connect to the database
+spring.datasource.password=S3cr3t-Pa55
$ git show HEAD~3:src/main/resources/application.properties | tail -1
spring.datasource.password=S3cr3t-Pa55
$ git count-objects -vH | grep -E "^(count|size)"
count: 25
size: 4.87 MiB
size-pack: 0 bytes
size-garbage: 0 bytes
blocks.title: A new commit does not remove the old content

blocks.text: After the "fix" commit (which moved the password to an environment variable and stopped tracking the jar), the old commit still contains the password and the object database still holds 4.87 MiB. Removing both requires rewriting every commit. The recommended tool is `git filter-repo` (a separate Python program; it was not installed on the build machine and the commands below that use it are **not run**):

blocks.code:
# remove a file or directory from all history
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path orders-service.jar
# replace text in all history; expressions.txt contains lines such as
#   S3cr3t-Pa55==>REMOVED
git filter-repo --replace-text expressions.txt
blocks.title: git filter-repo (illustrative, not run on the build machine)

blocks.text: The built-in `git filter-branch` performs the same rewrite (it is slow and officially discouraged in favour of `filter-repo`, and it prints a deprecation warning that the session below suppressed with `FILTER_BRANCH_SQUELCH_WARNING=1`). The following session ran for real:

blocks.code:
$ git filter-branch -f --index-filter \
    'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch -q orders-service.jar' -- --all
Ref 'refs/heads/main' was rewritten
$ git filter-branch -f --tree-filter \
    "sed -i 's/S3cr3t-Pa55/REMOVED/' src/main/resources/application.properties \
    2>/dev/null || true" -- --all
Ref 'refs/heads/main' was rewritten
$ git log --oneline
c6e2628 Move password to environment variable; stop tracking jar
36fbe07 Add Order
b6b5215 Add built jar
6a2ecf5 Connect to the database
2f57817 Add configuration
$ git show HEAD~3:src/main/resources/application.properties | tail -1
spring.datasource.password=REMOVED
$ git reflog expire --expire=now --all
$ rm -rf .git/refs/original
$ git gc --prune=now -q
$ git count-objects -vH | grep -E "^(count|size|in-pack|size-pack)"
count: 0
size: 0 bytes
in-pack: 23
size-pack: 3.27 KiB
size-garbage: 0 bytes
$ git log --all --oneline -S"S3cr3t" | wc -l
0
blocks.title: Rewriting history with filter-branch, then pruning (progress lines omitted)

blocks.text: Every commit id after the first changed (`506ebf6` became `6a2ecf5`) because the content of each tree changed, and the object database shrank from 4.87 MiB to 3.27 KiB. Three clean-up steps follow the rewrite: delete `.git/refs/original` (where `filter-branch` keeps a backup), expire the reflog, and run `git gc --prune=now`. Without them the old objects remain on disk.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Rewriting local history does not recover a secret that has been pushed. A pushed secret must be treated as compromised from the moment of the push: clones, forks, CI logs, caches, mirrors and the hosting provider's cached views may still contain it. The first action is to revoke or rotate the credential. History rewriting is a clean-up step, not a remedy. GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) states that for a secret the first step is to revoke or rotate it, and that after a rewrite and a forced push of all refs, cached views and pull-request refs may remain until GitHub Support removes them; clones and forks held by others cannot be cleaned remotely.

blocks.text:
### Hands-on

1. Create commits `one`, `two`, `three`; branch `temp` at `three`, add commit `four` on it, switch to `main` and run `git branch` `-D temp`. Find `four` in `git reflog` and recreate a branch at it.
2. Run `git reset --hard HEAD~2` on `main`, then restore the tip with `git reflog` and `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`.
3. Run `git switch --detach HEAD~1`, commit a file, run `git switch main`, read the warning, and save the commit with `git branch saved <id>`.
4. Commit `head -c 1000000 /dev/urandom > big.bin`, delete it in a second commit, note `git count-objects -vH`, remove it with `git filter-branch --index-filter 'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch -q big.bin' --` `--all`, expire the reflog, remove `.git/refs/original`, run `git gc --prune=now`, and compare the size.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: application.properties with the database password was committed and pushed

**Scenario.** A developer commits `application.properties` with `spring.datasource.password=...` and pushes the branch to GitHub. A reviewer notices the password in the pull request.

**Symptoms.** The password appears in the diff of the pull request and in `git log -p`. GitHub secret scanning may send an alert if the secret has a recognised format.

**Diagnosis.** `git log -p -S"<password>" --all` lists every commit that added or removed the string. `git grep` `"<password>" $(git rev-list --all)` searches the content of all commits (slow on large histories).

**Root cause.** The configuration file with real values was tracked. Moving the value to an environment variable in a later commit does not remove it from earlier commits.

**Fix.** (1) Rotate the database password immediately and update the deployment. (2) Replace the value in the file with a placeholder such as `${DB_PASSWORD}` and commit. (3) If the branch has not been merged, rewrite it (`git rebase -i`, or `filter-repo --replace-text`) and force-push with `--force-with-lease`; if it has, decide with the team whether a history rewrite of `main` is worth the disruption, since the rotation already neutralised the secret. (4) Check the database audit log for use of the old password.

**Prevention.** Keep secrets out of the repository: environment variables, Spring configuration from a secret store, `application-local.properties` in `.gitignore`. Enable GitHub push protection (see the chapter on GitHub) and a pre-commit scan (see the chapter on hooks).

#### Problem: commits made in detached HEAD disappeared

**Scenario.** A developer checks out a tag to reproduce a customer defect, fixes it, commits twice, then switches back to `main` and finds the work missing.

**Symptoms.** `git log` on every branch lacks the commits; `git branch` shows no trace. Git printed a warning on switching away that was not read.

**Diagnosis.** `git reflog` lists the commits as `commit: ...` entries between the checkout of the tag and the checkout of `main`.

**Root cause.** Commits made in detached HEAD are referenced only by HEAD; moving HEAD away leaves them unreachable.

**Fix.** `git branch rescued <id>` using the id from the warning or from `git reflog`, as shown in the worked example. Do this before the reflog entry expires.

**Prevention.** Create a branch first (`git switch -c hotfix/null-customer v1.0.0` starts a branch at a tag), and treat the warning on leaving a detached HEAD as an instruction.

#### Problem: the repository grew to hundreds of megabytes after a jar was committed

**Scenario.** `target/orders-service.jar` was committed in an early commit. The repository is huge, and CI clones take minutes.

**Symptoms.** `git count-objects -vH` shows a large `size-pack`; the object listing in the previous chapter shows a large blob.

**Diagnosis.** The `rev-list | cat-file --batch-check` pipeline from the data-model chapter ranks blobs by size and prints the path.

**Root cause.** A binary was committed; each version of a binary is stored whole (deltas help little with compressed files).

**Fix.** Rewrite history with `git filter-repo --invert-paths --path target/` (or the `filter-branch` form shown above), expire the reflog, garbage collect, force-push all branches and tags, and ask all collaborators to re-clone. Measured effect in the worked example: 4.87 MiB down to 3.27 KiB for a 5 MB file. On GitHub, cached data remains until Support removes it, as the documentation notes.

**Prevention.** Ignore build output; store binaries in a Maven or container registry; use Git LFS for unavoidable large assets. A pre-receive size limit or a CI check on blob sizes catches mistakes early.

### Questions to expect

#### How can a deleted branch be recovered?

Find the last commit of the branch with `git reflog` (or from the id printed by `git branch -D`) and create a branch there: `git branch <name> <id>`.

#### How is `git reset --hard` undone?

If the discarded work was committed, use `git reflog` and `git reset --hard HEAD@{n}` (or `ORIG_HEAD`). Uncommitted work discarded by `--hard` cannot be recovered by Git.

#### What is a detached HEAD and why is it dangerous?

HEAD points directly at a commit. New commits are referenced only by HEAD and become unreachable when HEAD moves, so a branch must be created to keep them.

#### How is a pushed commit undone?

With `git revert`, which adds a commit that reverses it. Rewriting shared history with reset and a force push is possible but disrupts every collaborator.

#### A password was committed and pushed. What are the steps?

Revoke and rotate the credential, check the audit logs, remove it from the current files, optionally rewrite history with `git filter-repo` and force-push, contact the host about cached views, and tell collaborators to re-clone or rebase. Rotation is the only step that actually removes the risk.

#### Why is the secret still compromised after history is rewritten?

Clones, forks, CI logs and caches that already exist hold the old objects, and the hosting service may serve cached commit views. The rewrite does not reach those copies.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Committed work is rarely lost: the reflog, `ORIG_HEAD` and `git fsck --lost-found` find unreachable commits until garbage collection.

- Recover a branch with `git branch <name> <id>`; undo `reset --hard` with `reset --hard HEAD@{1}`.
- Never commit in a detached HEAD without creating a branch.
- Use `git revert` for pushed commits; use `filter-repo` only when history must be rewritten.
- A pushed secret is compromised: revoke and rotate first; history rewriting is secondary clean-up.

A repository on one laptop is a backup waiting to fail and a team of one. Collaboration needs a shared repository to which every developer can send commits and from which every developer can receive the commits of the others. Git models this with **remotes**: named references to other repositories, with **remote-tracking branches** that record the last known state of the branches there. All shared-repository operations (clone, fetch, pull, push) are transfers of objects and updates of references between two repositories. This chapter simulates a team on one machine, using a *bare repository* as the server and two clones as the developers, and shows the exact messages of a rejected push, a conflicting `git pull --rebase`, a diverged pull and a force push that destroyed a colleague's commit.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Remotes, remote-tracking branches and tracking

`git clone <url>` creates a new repository, stores the source as the remote named `origin`, downloads all objects, creates one **remote-tracking branch** for each remote branch (`origin/main`), and checks out a local branch `main` that **tracks** `origin/main`. A remote-tracking branch is a local reference under `refs/remotes/origin/`. It can only be moved by `git fetch`, `git pull` or `git push`, never by committing; it records what the remote looked like at the last contact. A local branch with an *upstream* (`branch.main.remote` and `branch.main.merge` in `.git/config`) lets `git status` report "ahead 1, behind 2", and lets `git pull` and `git push` run without arguments.

blocks.text:
#### fetch, pull and push

`git fetch` downloads new objects and updates the remote-tracking branches; it never changes local branches or the working tree, so it is always safe. `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by `git merge` of the upstream branch, or by `git` `rebase` when configured with `--rebase` or `pull.rebase=true`. `git push <remote> <branch>` uploads the objects the remote lacks and asks the remote to move its branch to the local tip.

The remote accepts a push only if it is a **fast-forward** of the remote branch: the new tip must contain the old tip as an ancestor. Otherwise the push is **rejected** (`non-fast-forward`), because accepting it would discard commits that others pushed. The rule protects shared work; the developer must integrate the remote changes first. A **force push** (`--force`) overrides the check and moves the remote branch to the sent commit, discarding whatever it pointed to. `--force-with-lease` overrides the check only if the remote branch still points to the commit that the local remote-tracking branch recorded, that is, if nobody has pushed since the last fetch.

#### Bare repositories, forks and upstream

A **bare repository** has no working tree; it contains only what is normally inside `.git`. It is what a server (GitHub, GitLab, a company SSH server) stores, and `git init --bare` creates one. A **fork** is a server-side copy of a repository under another account, used when the original is not writable. A local clone of a fork conventionally names the fork `origin` and the original repository `upstream`, so that `git fetch upstream` brings the original's changes.

#### Transport and authentication

Git speaks to remotes over **HTTPS** (`https://host/owner/repo.git`), **SSH** (`git@host:owner/repo.git`) or the local file system. With HTTPS the client authenticates with a username and a token (GitHub removed account-password authentication for Git operations in 2021, from memory, and documents personal access tokens for this purpose) cached by a credential helper. With SSH the client holds a private key and the server holds the public key; no secret travels over the network and no password is typed. SSH is the usual choice for a developer's own machine; HTTPS with tokens or short-lived credentials is typical for automation. The details of keys and tokens are in the chapter on GitHub.

blocks.text:
### Worked example

#### A bare remote and two clones

The remote is a bare repository `origin.git`. Two developers, Asha and Maruthi, each have a clone.

blocks.code:
$ git init --bare --initial-branch=main origin.git
Initialized empty Git repository in /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git/
$ git clone origin.git asha
Cloning into 'asha'...
warning: You appear to have cloned an empty repository.
done.
$ cd asha
$ echo '# orders-service' > README.md && git add -A && git commit -m "Initial commit"
$ git push -u origin main
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
$ git branch -vv
* main 7a2df8b [origin/main] Initial commit
$ grep -A3 -E '^\[(remote|branch)' .git/config
[remote "origin"]
        url = /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
        fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*
[branch "main"]
        remote = origin
        merge = refs/heads/main
blocks.title: Creating the remote and the first clone

blocks.text:
`-u` (`--set-upstream`) wrote the `[branch "main"]` section, which makes later `git push` and `git pull` argument-free. The `fetch` line of the remote is the **refspec** `+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*`: it maps each branch of the remote to a remote-tracking branch; the leading `+` allows non-fast-forward updates of those tracking branches.

#### A rejected push

Both developers clone, and then each makes a different commit on `main`. Asha pushes first. The push of the second developer is rejected.

blocks.code:
$ git push
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
   7a2df8b..8409eef  main -> main
$ git push
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to '/tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull' before pushing again.
hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.
blocks.title: The second push is rejected as non-fast-forward

blocks.text:
The first block of output is Asha's successful push (`7a2df8b..8409eef`); the second is Maruthi's rejected one. `(fetch` `first)` means that the remote has commits unknown to the local repository. The sequence is summarised in the diagram.

**Asha origin Maruthi** **clone bare repo clone**

main = 7a2df8b on all three

push 8409eef

ok: 7a2df8b..8409eef

push df06810 (parent 7a2df8b)

rejected: fetch first

git fetch

origin/main = 8409eef

git pull --rebase: replay df06810

push eb0b226 (parent 8409eef)

ok: 8409eef..eb0b226

*Figure 1.17. Observe that the rejection arrives before any data is written to origin, and that integration through* `git pull --rebase` *produces a commit whose parent is the remote tip, so the next push is a fast-forward.*

#### fetch, inspect, integrate

blocks.code:
$ git fetch
From /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin
   7a2df8b..8409eef  main       -> origin/main
$ git status -sb
## main...origin/main [ahead 1, behind 1]
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
* 8409eef Document run steps
| * df06810 Document build steps
|/
* 7a2df8b Initial commit

blocks.title: Fetching first, then looking at the difference

blocks.text: `ahead 1, behind 1` is the signature of diverged histories. Both commits appended a line to the same final line of `README.md`, so `git pull --rebase` conflicts while replaying Maruthi's commit:

blocks.code:
$ git pull --rebase
Auto-merging README.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md
