Asha line
=======
Maruthi line
>>>>>>> df06810 (Document build steps)
blocks.title: A conflict during git pull --rebase

blocks.text: During a rebase the labels are reversed relative to a merge: `HEAD` (the upper block) is the upstream commit being rebuilt on, here Asha's work, and the lower block belongs to the commit being replayed (Maruthi's). Git is detached at that moment (`HEAD (no branch)`). After editing the file to contain both lines the rebase is continued.

blocks.code:
$ git add README.md
$ git rebase --continue
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
* eb0b226 Document build steps
* 8409eef Document run steps
* 7a2df8b Initial commit
$ git push
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git

blocks.title: Finishing the rebase and pushing

#### Diverged branches and the pull configuration

With default settings Git 2.43 refuses a `git pull` of diverged branches until the reconciliation method is chosen:

blocks.code:

$ git pull

blocks.text:
#### force-with-lease against force

Maruthi pushes a feature branch `feature/tidy`; Asha adds a review fix on the same branch and pushes; Maruthi amends his commit and tries to push.

blocks.code:
$ git push -u origin feature/tidy
 * [new branch]      feature/tidy -> feature/tidy
branch 'feature/tidy' set up to track 'origin/feature/tidy'.
$ git commit --amend -m "Tidy 1 (reworded)"
$ git push --force origin feature/tidy --dry-run
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
 + a6c9c4a...810eef6 feature/tidy -> feature/tidy (forced update)
$ git push --force-with-lease origin feature/tidy
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
 ! [rejected]        feature/tidy -> feature/tidy (stale info)
error: failed to push some refs to '/tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git'
$ git fetch
From /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin
   0121c96..a6c9c4a  feature/tidy -> origin/feature/tidy
$ git push --force-with-lease origin feature/tidy
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
 + a6c9c4a...810eef6 feature/tidy -> feature/tidy (forced update)
blocks.title: Force versus force-with-lease

blocks.text:
The dry run shows that a plain `--force` would have replaced Asha's commit `a6c9c4a`. The first `--force-with-lease` was rejected with `stale info`, because the remote branch had moved since the last fetch. The second one succeeded and **did overwrite Asha's commit**: after `git fetch`, the local remote-tracking branch pointed at `a6c9c4a`, so the lease was satisfied, although the commit had not been looked at. The lease protects against unseen changes only; running `git fetch` and then pushing without inspecting the result defeats it. The consequences for Asha are shown in the problem section below.

#### Fork and upstream

After `git remote add upstream <url>`, `git fetch upstream` creates `upstream/main` and `upstream/feature/tidy`, and `git merge --ff-only upstream/main` brought a new upstream commit into the fork's local `main` (`Fast-forward`, one file changed). The test used two local bare repositories in place of `fork.git` and `upstream.git`; on GitHub they are repositories of two accounts and the fork button performs the copy.

### Hands-on

1. Create `shared.git` with `git init --bare --initial-branch=main`, clone it twice as `dev1` and `dev2` with different `user.name` values, commit `A.txt` in `dev1` and push with `-u`; run `git pull` in `dev2`.
2. Edit the same line of `A.txt` differently in both clones and commit. Push from `dev1`; predict, then observe, the message on `git push` from `dev2`. Run `git fetch`, `git status -sb` and `git log --oneline --graph --all`, then `git pull --rebase`, resolve, `git rebase --continue` and push.
3. On a branch pushed by both clones, amend a commit in `dev1` and compare `git push --force-with-lease` before and after `git fetch`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a force push overwrote a teammate's commit

**Scenario.** After the sequence in the worked example, Asha's review fix is missing from `origin/feature/tidy`.

**Symptoms.** On Asha's machine `git fetch` prints `(forced update)`, and `git status -sb` shows the branch as `ahead` `2, behind 1`.

**Diagnosis.** Asha's clone still contains the lost commit:

blocks.code:
$ git fetch
From /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin
 + a6c9c4a...810eef6 feature/tidy -> origin/feature/tidy  (forced update)
$ git status -sb
## feature/tidy...origin/feature/tidy [ahead 2, behind 1]
$ git log --oneline --graph --all -6
* a6c9c4a Review fix from Asha
* 0121c96 Tidy 1
| * 810eef6 Tidy 1 (reworded)
|/
* eb0b226 Document build steps
* 8409eef Document run steps
* 7a2df8b Initial commit
blocks.title: Seeing the forced update and finding the lost commit

blocks.text: **Root cause.** A force push replaced the remote branch tip. The pusher had amended a commit (new id `810eef6`) and sent it with a lease that had been refreshed by `git fetch`. **Fix.** The naive `git pull --rebase` is a trap here. In the test it printed `Successfully rebased` and dropped *both* of Asha's local commits, because Git's fork-point detection saw them in the reflog of `origin/feature/tidy` and treated them as already integrated upstream. The review fix was gone from the branch but still present in the reflog, from where it was copied back:

blocks.code:
$ git reflog -5
810eef6 HEAD@{0}: pull --rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature/tidy
810eef6 HEAD@{1}: pull --rebase (start): checkout 810eef699c85508d7febbea09e5f2b2f289d6bd5
a6c9c4a HEAD@{2}: commit: Review fix from Asha
0121c96 HEAD@{3}: checkout: moving from main to feature/tidy
8409eef HEAD@{4}: commit: Document run steps
$ git cherry-pick a6c9c4a
[feature/tidy 8c57e03] Review fix from Asha
 Date: Thu Oct 1 10:33:00 2026 +0530
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 review.txt
$ git push
To /tmp/dvw_v1/work/rem/origin.git
   810eef6..8c57e03  feature/tidy -> feature/tidy
blocks.title: Recovering the dropped commit from the reflog

blocks.text:
Before pulling after a forced update, `git log --oneline --graph --all` should be read to decide which local commits are really new (here only `a6c9c4a`; `0121c96` is the old version of the amended commit). A deliberate alternative to the automatic rebase is `git reset --hard origin/feature/tidy` followed by `git cherry-pick` of those commits. The lost commit remains in the reflog of the clone that created it.

**Prevention.** Do not force-push to branches that others use; protect shared branches against force pushes (GitHub branch protection or rulesets); use `--force-with-lease` and look at what `git fetch` brought before pushing; agree that only the branch owner rewrites a branch.

#### Problem: the local and remote histories have diverged

**Scenario.** `git push` is rejected, and `git pull` prints `fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent` `branches`.

**Symptoms.** `git status -sb` shows `ahead N, behind M` with both numbers non-zero.

**Diagnosis.** `git fetch` followed by `git log --oneline --graph --all` and `git diff main origin/main --stat` shows what each side has.

**Root cause.** Two people committed on the same branch from the same starting point. This is normal in collaboration and is not an error in itself.

**Fix.** Integrate, then push: `git pull --rebase` (linear history, replayed local commits) or `git pull --no-rebase` (merge commit). Set the policy once with `git config --global pull.rebase true` or `pull.ff only`. On conflict, resolve and `git rebase --continue`. **Do not** answer the rejection with `git push --force`; that discards the remote commits.

**Prevention.** Run `git pull --rebase` before starting work and before pushing, use short-lived feature branches instead of committing directly to a shared branch, and protect `main` so that all changes arrive through pull requests.

### Questions to expect

#### What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?

`fetch` downloads objects and updates remote-tracking branches only. `pull` is `fetch` followed by a merge (or rebase) into the current branch, so it can change the working tree and cause conflicts.

#### What is a remote-tracking branch?

A local read-only reference such as `origin/main` that records the state of a branch on a remote at the last fetch. It moves only through fetch, pull or push.

#### Why was my push rejected as non-fast-forward?

The remote branch contains commits that the local branch does not. Accepting the push would drop them. Fetch, integrate (rebase or merge) and push again.

#### What is the difference between `--force` and `--force-with-lease`?

`--force` overwrites the remote branch unconditionally. `--force-with-lease` overwrites only if the remote branch still equals the local remote-tracking branch, so a push from a colleague after the last fetch aborts it. It is safer but does not help if the fetch result was not examined.

#### What is a bare repository?

A repository without a working tree, used as a central or server repository. `git init --bare` creates one; pushing to the checked-out branch of a non-bare repository is refused for the same reason.

#### What is a fork and what is `upstream`?

A fork is a server-side copy of a repository under another account. By convention the local remote `origin` points at the fork and `upstream` at the original, so that `git fetch upstream` retrieves its new commits.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A remote is a named URL; remote-tracking branches record its last known state; only fetch, pull and push update them.

- A push must be a fast-forward of the remote branch; otherwise it is rejected until the remote work is integrated.
- `git pull` equals fetch plus merge or rebase; configure `pull.rebase` explicitly.
- Avoid force pushes to shared branches; `--force-with-lease` helps only when fetch results are inspected.
- Use SSH keys on workstations and tokens over HTTPS for automation; never put credentials in remote URLs that are committed.

A branching strategy is an agreement on which branches exist, who may commit to them, how work reaches production and how releases are named. Git does not prescribe one. The choice affects review practice, release frequency, the cost of integration and the tools that are needed (feature flags, release branches, continuous integration). This chapter describes the three strategies in common use, the supporting practices (commit conventions, semantic versioning, tagging, changelogs, feature flags, merge queues, repository layout) and a decision guide, all in terms of the `orders-service` repository.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Git Flow

Git Flow was published by Vincent Driessen in 2010 (from memory; the author later added a note to the original article recommending simpler workflows for continuously delivered software). It uses long-lived branches `main` (released code, every merge tagged) and `develop` (integration of the next release), plus short-lived `feature/*` branches from `develop`, `release/*` branches for stabilising a version, and `hotfix/*` branches from `main` for urgent production fixes. A release branch is merged into both `main` and `develop`; a hotfix likewise.

blocks.text:
Git Flow suits software with explicit versions and several supported releases (libraries, mobile applications, on-premises products). Its cost is the overhead of two permanent branches and the delay between a change and its release. For a service deployed continuously, such as `orders-service`, it is usually heavier than needed.

#### GitHub Flow

GitHub Flow uses a single permanent branch, `main`, which must always be deployable. Per GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) the steps are: create a branch; make changes and push; open a pull request (a draft for early feedback); review; merge after approval and required checks; delete the branch. The documentation recommends short descriptive branch names and one branch per set of unrelated changes.

#### Trunk-based development

In trunk-based development all developers integrate into one branch (the *trunk*, normally `main`) at least daily, through very short-lived branches (a day or two) or direct commits protected by fast automated checks. Unfinished work is merged but hidden behind a **feature flag** so that it is deployed but not released. Release branches are optional and short-lived: they are cut from the trunk to stabilise a release, and fixes are made on the trunk first and cherry-picked. Teams with strong automated testing and continuous delivery tend to choose this model; its weakness is the dependence on that test suite and on disciplined small changes.

blocks.caption: Branching strategies compared.

blocks.text:
#### Feature flags

A **feature flag** (feature toggle) is a runtime condition that switches behaviour on or off without a deployment. It separates *deploying* code from *releasing* a feature: the code reaches production switched off, and is enabled for a subset of users or for everyone later, and disabled again at once if it misbehaves. Flags add code paths that must be tested in both states and must be removed when the feature is permanent; old flags are a common source of defects.

#### Release branches and hotfixes

A **release branch** (`release/1.4`) freezes a version while `main` continues. Only fixes go to the release branch; each fix is made on `main` first and cherry-picked, so that no fix is lost on the next release. A **hotfix** is a fix for production that cannot wait: branch from the tag of the running release, fix, tag a patch version (`v1.4.1`), deploy, and make sure the same change is on `main`. The classic failure is a hotfix that never reaches `main`, so the next release contains the defect again.

#### Monorepo or polyrepo

A **monorepo** holds many services and libraries in one repository; a **polyrepo** holds one repository per service. A monorepo gives atomic cross-service changes, one place for shared tooling and simple code sharing, but needs build tooling that builds only what changed, scales the repository and CI cost, and requires fine-grained access control. A polyrepo gives clear ownership, independent histories and pipelines, and simple permissions, but cross-cutting changes need coordinated pull requests and versioned libraries. For a handful of Spring Boot services owned by one team either works; the decisive factors are team boundaries and the build tooling available.

#### Merge queue

On a busy `main`, two pull requests can each pass checks and still break the build when combined. A **merge queue** (GitHub feature) tests each pull request on top of the latest `main` plus the pull requests queued before it, and merges only if the checks pass. Per GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) checks must run on the `merge_group` event, a merge queue is enabled through a branch protection rule or ruleset, and it is available for public repositories owned by an organisation and for private repositories on GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

#### Commit conventions and Conventional Commits

A shared message format makes history readable and allows tools to generate changelogs and version numbers. The **Conventional Commits** specification (version 1.0.0, consulted October 2026) defines the structure `type[(scope)][!]: description`, an optional body and optional footers. `fix` corresponds to a PATCH release, `feat` to a MINOR release, and a breaking change (marked with `!` after the type or scope, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer) to a MAJOR release; other types such as `docs`, `chore`, `refactor`, `test` and `ci` are allowed and by themselves do not change the version.

#### Semantic versioning and tagging releases

**Semantic Versioning** (semver.org, version 2.0.0; from memory) names a version `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`: MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for compatible additions, PATCH for compatible fixes; a suffix such as `-SNAPSHOT` (Maven convention) or `-rc.1` marks a pre-release. A release is recorded as an annotated tag (`v1.4.0`) on the exact commit that was built; the tag is the link between a running artifact, its container image tag and the source. Pushing the tag (`git push origin v1.4.0`) is typically what triggers a release pipeline (see the chapters on continuous delivery).

#### Changelogs and release notes

A changelog lists notable changes per version for users; release notes are the same for one release. Tools generate drafts from Conventional Commits or from merged pull-request titles and labels (GitHub can generate release notes automatically). Generated text is a draft: it must be edited for readers who did not see the commits.

### Worked example

#### Conventional Commits in the history

A history of four commits was created with conventional subjects, and a commit-message hook (shown in the chapter on hooks) rejected a non-conforming message.

blocks.code:
$ git commit -m "update stuff"; echo exit=$?
commit-msg: subject must look like 'type(scope): description'
exit=1
$ git commit -m "docs: describe local setup"; echo exit=$?
[main b78d98a] docs: describe local setup
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md
exit=0
blocks.title: Rejected and accepted messages

blocks.text: The subjects make the next version computable and the changelog extractable with plain `git log` and `grep`:

blocks.code:
$ git log --format="%s" | grep -E "^feat"
feat(auth)!: require JWT on all routes
feat(orders): add discount endpoint
$ git log --format="%s" | grep -E "^fix"
fix(orders): reject zero quantity
$ git log --format='%s' | grep -E '^[a-z]+(\([a-z0-9-]+\))?!:'
feat(auth)!: require JWT on all routes
blocks.title: Extracting changelog entries and the breaking change

blocks.text: One breaking `feat` commit means the next release is a MAJOR version according to the specification, for example from `1.3.2` to `2.0.0`. A tag records it:

blocks.code:
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m "Release 2.0.0: JWT required on all routes"
git push origin v2.0.0

#### A feature flag in Java

The following program implements a flag read from an environment variable, which is how a containerised Spring Boot service can receive it (`FEATURE_NEW_DISCOUNT=true` set in the container or the Kubernetes manifest; in a Spring application the equivalent is a configuration property).

blocks.title: FlagDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java FlagDemo.java
price = 200.0
$ FEATURE_NEW_DISCOUNT=true java FlagDemo.java
price = 180.0
blocks.title: Flag off, then flag on

blocks.text:
The code is deployed in both runs; only the environment decides which path runs. A default of `false` makes an unset flag safe. Production systems usually read flags from a configuration service so that they can be changed without restarting.

### Hands-on

1. Build the Git Flow graph: create `develop`, a `feature/a` merged with `--no-ff`, a `release/1.0` merged into `main` with `--no-ff` and tagged `v1.0.0`, and merged back into `develop`; compare `git log --oneline --graph --all` with the diagram. Then start `hotfix/x` from the tag, tag `v1.0.1`, and merge it into both branches (`git branch --contains` `<commit>` must list both).
2. Write a script that reads `git log --format=%s v1.0.0..HEAD` and prints the next semantic version: MAJOR when a subject matches `!:`, MINOR when one starts with `feat`, otherwise PATCH.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: a hotfix was released but never reached main

**Scenario.** A defect in `orders-service` 1.4.0 is fixed on `hotfix/null-customer`, tagged `v1.4.1` and deployed. Two weeks later release 1.5.0 reintroduces the defect.

**Symptoms.** The same issue reappears in a new release; `git log main` lacks the hotfix commit.

**Diagnosis.** `git branch --contains <hotfix-commit>` lists which branches hold the fix; `git log --oneline` `main..v1.4.1` lists commits in the release that are not on `main`.

**Root cause.** The hotfix branch was merged only into the release line (or only tagged). The fix existed on one branch, and `main` continued without it.

**Fix.** Cherry-pick or merge the hotfix commit into `main` now (`git cherry-pick <id>`), add a regression test, and release a patch. **Prevention.** Adopt the rule "fix on main first, then cherry-pick to the release branch" (trunk-based) or "hotfix merges into both main and develop" (Git Flow), and add a CI check that fails when `git log main..release/x` contains fix commits that are absent from `main`.

### Questions to expect

#### Compare Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development.

Git Flow keeps `main` and `develop` and uses feature, release and hotfix branches, which suits versioned products. GitHub Flow keeps a single deployable `main` and merges short branches through pull requests. Trunk-based development integrates into one branch at least daily and hides unfinished work behind feature flags. Strong automated testing is a prerequisite for the last two.

#### What is a hotfix and how is it handled?

An urgent production fix. Branch from the released tag, fix, tag a patch version, deploy, and ensure the fix is also on `main` (and `develop` in Git Flow).

#### What is Semantic Versioning and how do Conventional Commits relate to it?

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` with rules for incompatible, compatible and fix changes. Conventional Commits map `fix` to PATCH, `feat` to MINOR and breaking changes to MAJOR, so tools can compute the version.

#### What is a merge queue?

A mechanism that tests each pull request against the latest target branch plus the queued changes before merging, which prevents a green-individually, red-together `main`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Choose the lightest strategy that the test and release automation can support: GitHub Flow or trunk-based for services, Git Flow for versioned products.

- Feature flags separate deploy from release; they need owners and removal dates.
- Hotfixes and release-branch fixes must always reach `main`.
- Conventional Commits and Semantic Versioning make versions and changelogs computable; tag every release with an annotated tag.
- A merge queue prevents combinations of individually valid pull requests from breaking `main`.

Git moves commits between repositories; it has no notion of review, approval, discussion or automated checks. A team needs those, and GitHub is the hosting service that supplies them on top of Git: repositories, pull requests, access control, issue tracking, release pages, a package registry, dependency and secret scanning, static-site hosting and a workflow engine (GitHub Actions, covered in the part on continuous integration). GitLab and Bitbucket offer comparable features under different names. This chapter explains the features that a backend developer uses daily, with configuration files that can be committed to a repository. Product behaviour that was verified against the GitHub documentation is marked `consulted October 2026`; the web interface changes often, and interface steps are described by feature name rather than by screen position. **GitHub itself is not available on the build machine**, so every GitHub-side step in this chapter is illustrative (not run); the YAML files were syntax-checked with PyYAML (`yaml.safe_load` succeeded) and the Git commands elsewhere in the guide were run for real.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Repository files that GitHub recognises

A repository on GitHub is a Git repository plus metadata. Several files at the root or in a `.github/` directory are interpreted by the service.

blocks.caption: Files with a special meaning on GitHub.

blocks.text:
According to the GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026), a pull request template can be placed in the repository root, in `docs/` or in `.github/`, and a `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` subdirectory allows several templates, chosen by a `template` query parameter in the URL. Issue form files are YAML files in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE`. `CODEOWNERS` is searched in `.github/`, the root and `docs/`, in that order, and the first file found is used.

#### The pull request

A **pull request** (PR) proposes merging one branch into another and is the unit of review. It shows the diff, the commits, the discussion, and the results of automated checks. The lifecycle follows the GitHub Flow steps described in the previous chapter.

A repository administrator can allow only some of these. With squash merging, the pull request title becomes the commit subject, which is why teams that use Conventional Commits require the PR title to follow the convention.

#### Code review practice

Review is the practice that most improves quality and shares knowledge. Reviewers read for correctness first, then design, tests, security and readability; the author keeps changes small (a few hundred changed lines at most), describes *why* the change is needed, links the issue, and shows evidence of testing. Comments state the observation and the reason, distinguish blocking from optional points, and are answered with either a change or an explanation. A reviewer checklist for a Spring Boot service:

1. The pull request does one thing and its description explains the reason.
2. The build and tests pass; new behaviour has tests, including the failure path.
3. Public API changes (endpoints, DTOs, database schema) are backward compatible, or the migration is described.
4. No secrets, personal data or environment-specific values are committed; configuration keys are documented.
5. Input is validated, errors are handled and logged without sensitive data, and transactions and queries are reasonable.
6. Dependencies added to `pom.xml` are necessary, maintained and compatible with the licence policy.
7. Naming and structure follow the project conventions; no dead code or commented-out blocks remain.

#### Branch protection, rulesets and required checks

A **branch protection rule** enforces conditions on a branch such as `main`. According to GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) the options include: require a pull request with a number of approving reviews, optionally from code owners; require status checks to pass, optionally with the branch up to date with the base; require conversation resolution; require signed commits; require linear history; require a merge queue; lock the branch; restrict who can push; allow or forbid force pushes and deletions (both off by default); and apply the rules to administrators. The documentation also notes that only one branch protection rule can apply to a branch at a time, that **rulesets** do not have this limitation, and that existing rules can be converted to rulesets.

blocks.text:
A **required status check** is a named check, usually a job of a GitHub Actions workflow, that must succeed before merging. The name in the rule must match the name reported by the job. If a workflow does not run for a pull request (for example because a path filter excluded it), the required check never reports and the pull request waits indefinitely; this is a frequent source of confusion and is treated in the problems of this chapter. Checks used by a merge queue must also run on the `merge_group` event.

#### CODEOWNERS

`CODEOWNERS` assigns reviewers by path using gitignore-style patterns. Per the documentation (consulted October 2026), the last matching pattern wins, owners are users or teams with write access, and a branch protection rule that requires review from code owners makes the approval of any one listed owner mandatory. Protecting the file itself is done by assigning an owner to it.

#### Issues, labels, projects and templates

**Issues** track bugs and tasks; **labels** classify them (`bug`, `enhancement`, `good first issue`); **milestones** group them by release; **Projects** provide a board or table over issues and pull requests. An **issue form** (a YAML file) collects structured input and makes required fields mandatory, which reduces incomplete reports. Closing keywords in a pull request description (`Fixes #42`) link the pull request to the issue and close it on merge.

#### Releases and packages

A **GitHub Release** is attached to a Git tag. Per GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) a release can be created from an existing or new tag, can be saved as a draft or marked as a pre-release, can include automatically generated release notes, and can be created by users with write access. Release assets (a jar, checksums) are attached to it. The **package registry** (GitHub Packages) hosts container images at `ghcr.io` and Maven artifacts; its use in a pipeline appears in the chapters on GitHub Actions.

#### Dependency and secret security

**Dependabot** has three functions: alerts for vulnerable dependencies, automatic security update pull requests, and scheduled version update pull requests configured in `.github/dependabot.yml`. **Secret scanning** detects known credential formats in a repository; **push protection** (per documentation, consulted October 2026) blocks a push that contains a detected secret, covers command-line pushes, web edits and uploads, can be bypassed by users with write access who give a reason (which creates an alert), and repository-level push protection requires the GitHub Secret Protection feature; availability depends on the plan and repository visibility, which should be checked in the current documentation. **Code scanning** (CodeQL) analyses source for vulnerabilities. These features appear on the repository's *Security* tab.

#### GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages is a static site hosting service that publishes HTML, CSS and JavaScript from a repository, optionally after a build (documentation consulted October 2026). A user or organisation may have one site in a repository named `<owner>.github.io`, and a project site per repository. It suits documentation and portfolios; it cannot run a Spring Boot application.

#### Authentication: SSH keys, tokens and the forking workflow

For SSH access a key pair is generated locally and the public key is added to the account. GitHub documents the Ed25519 algorithm (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "email"`), with `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as the default location and `ssh-add` to load the key into the agent. For HTTPS access, tokens replace passwords. According to GitHub documentation (consulted October 2026) **fine-grained personal access tokens** carry specific permissions, are limited to one resource owner and can be restricted to selected repositories, whereas **classic tokens** use broad scopes and can reach every repository that the user can access; GitHub recommends fine-grained tokens whenever possible and strongly recommends an expiration date. Some features, such as Packages, are not yet covered by fine-grained tokens. A leaked token has the same consequences as a leaked password: revoke it at once. Automation inside GitHub Actions uses the short-lived `GITHUB_TOKEN`, described in the pipeline chapters.

The **forking workflow** is used when the contributor has no write access, as in open source: fork, clone the fork, add the original as `upstream`, create a branch, push it to the fork, and open a pull request from the fork branch to the original.

#### Profile and portfolio advice for placements

Recruiters and interviewers often open a candidate's profile before the interview. A short checklist makes it effective:

- Pin four to six repositories that show finished, running work; archive or hide abandoned experiments.
- Give each pinned repository a README with a one-paragraph purpose, an architecture diagram, the technology list (Java 21, Spring Boot 3, PostgreSQL), exact build and run commands, and a screenshot or an API example.
- Show engineering practice: a pipeline badge, tests, a Dockerfile, a Compose file, meaningful commit messages and small pull requests (even when working alone, branches and pull requests demonstrate the workflow).
- Never leave secrets, `.env` files or personal data in history; a scan of the profile by an interviewer takes seconds.
- Keep the contribution record honest: a few well-maintained projects and one or two real contributions to open-source repositories weigh more than many empty ones.

A `.github/pull_request_template.md` file with the headings "What and why" (with `Fixes #`), "How it was tested" (checkboxes for unit tests, `mvn -B verify` and a manual check of `/actuator/health`) and "Checklist" (no secrets committed, database changes backward compatible, documentation updated) pre-fills every new pull request description and turns the review checklist above into a habit.

For GitHub Actions the documentation states that `/` makes Dependabot search `/.github/workflows`. The identifiers `maven` and `docker` were not confirmed in the excerpt that was consulted and should be checked against the reference before use. `open-pull-requests-limit` caps the number of simultaneously open update pull requests, which prevents a flood.

#### A workflow that supplies the required check

The required status check must come from a job with a stable name. The following minimal workflow reports a check named `build` for pull requests and for the merge queue.

blocks.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: "21"
          cache: maven
      - run: mvn -B verify
blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml

blocks.text:
The action versions `@v4` follow the pattern in the GitHub documentation examples but were **not re-verified for this** **chapter**; the chapters on GitHub Actions state the verified versions. The rule on `main` then lists `build` as a required status check.

### Hands-on

1. Create a repository and push the local example repository to it (`git remote add origin <url>`, `git push -u` `origin main`).
2. On a branch, add `CODEOWNERS`, the issue form, `dependabot.yml` and `ci.yml` from this chapter, open a pull request, and verify that the template fills the description.
3. After the first workflow run, protect `main` (a ruleset or a branch protection rule) with a required pull request, one approval and the status check `build`. Try `git push origin main` directly, record the error, and observe that the merge button of a pull request stays disabled until the check passes.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: the required check never reports and the pull request cannot merge

**Scenario.** `main` requires the check `build`. A pull request that changes only `README.md` shows `Expected - Waiting for` `status to be reported` and cannot be merged.

**Symptoms.** The merge box lists `build` as required but pending; no workflow run exists for the commit.

**Diagnosis.** The workflow has a path filter (`paths-ignore: ['**.md']`) or a branch filter, so it did not start; or the job name was changed and the rule still names the old one. The Actions tab shows no run for the pull request.

**Root cause.** A required check must be reported by some workflow; a skipped workflow reports nothing.

**Fix.** Remove the path filter from the workflow that provides a required check, or add a lightweight workflow with the same job name that always reports success for the excluded paths. After renaming a job, update the rule. Documentation for required checks and for skipped workflows (consulted at the time of use) gives the supported approaches.

**Prevention.** Name required jobs explicitly (`name: build`), avoid path filters on them, and review the list of required checks whenever workflows change.

#### Problem: CODEOWNERS is ignored or blocks every pull request

**Scenario.** After adding a `CODEOWNERS` file, reviews are not requested automatically, or no pull request can be merged because no eligible owner exists.

**Symptoms.** No reviewer is requested; or the merge box says `Review required` although approvals exist.

**Diagnosis.** The file is not at one of the three supported paths or is not on the base branch of the pull request; a listed owner lacks write access (invalid lines are skipped); a later broader pattern overrides a specific earlier one; or only one person owns a path and that person is the author of the pull request (authors cannot approve their own pull requests).

**Root cause.** Per the documentation (consulted October 2026) the file must be on the base branch, owners must have explicit write access, the last matching pattern takes precedence, and a missing or invalid owner means no valid review can satisfy the rule.

**Fix.** Move the file to `.github/CODEOWNERS`, give every listed team write access, order patterns from general to specific, and list at least two owners per path.

**Prevention.** Own directories with teams rather than individuals, and protect `CODEOWNERS` itself with an owner entry.

### Questions to expect

#### What is a pull request, and why is it used instead of pushing to main?

A request to merge a branch, shown with its diff, discussion and automated check results. It creates a point for review and testing before the change reaches the shared branch, and it leaves a durable record of the decision.

#### What do branch protection rules enforce?

Required pull requests and approvals, required status checks, resolved conversations, signed commits, linear history, restrictions on who can push, and prohibitions on force pushes and deletion, optionally also for administrators.

#### What is CODEOWNERS?

A file that maps paths to owners. When a pull request changes a path, the owners are requested as reviewers, and with the corresponding protection rule their approval is mandatory.

#### What do Dependabot and secret scanning do?

Dependabot raises alerts and opens pull requests that update vulnerable or outdated dependencies. Secret scanning detects credentials in the repository, and push protection blocks a push that contains one.

#### What is the difference between a fork and a branch?

A branch lives in the same repository and requires write access. A fork is a separate repository under another account, used by contributors without write access, who send changes back with a pull request.

#### Why prefer fine-grained tokens over classic tokens?

They are limited to chosen repositories and specific permissions and carry an expiry, so a leak has a smaller impact; classic tokens use broad scopes across all repositories the user can reach.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
GitHub adds review, protection and automation to Git; the pull request is the central unit.

- Protect `main` with required pull requests, reviews, status checks and CODEOWNERS; prefer rulesets for several overlapping rules.
- A required check must always report; path filters on required workflows block merges.
- Use Dependabot, secret scanning and push protection, but treat a pushed secret as compromised regardless.
- Prefer SSH keys or fine-grained tokens with expiry; use forks for contributions without write access.
- README, a pipeline badge, tests and clean history make a repository a credible portfolio item.

Three Git mechanisms complete the toolbox of a backend team. **Hooks** run scripts at defined points (before a commit, before a push) and catch errors before they reach the shared repository. **Attributes** (`.gitattributes`) control how Git treats particular paths: line endings, binary files, diff and merge behaviour. **Submodules** embed one repository inside another at a pinned commit. All three are configuration that lives in or next to the repository, and all three produce problems that look mysterious until the mechanism is known.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Hooks

A hook is an executable file with a fixed name. Git runs it at a specific event and, for most hooks, aborts the operation when the hook exits with a non-zero status. Hooks live in `.git/hooks/` by default (the directory contains `*.sample` files after `git init`) and are **not part of the repository**: they are not cloned. To share hooks, a team commits them to a directory such as `.githooks/` and sets `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, a setting that is also local and must be repeated by each clone (for example in a setup script or the Maven build).

blocks.text:
Client-side hooks are a convenience, not a control: `git commit --no-verify` and `git push --no-verify` skip them, and nobody is forced to install them. Policy that must hold (tests pass, no secrets, naming) is therefore repeated on the server side, in required status checks and branch protection. Hooks give fast feedback; the pipeline gives enforcement.

#### .gitattributes

`.gitattributes` assigns attributes to path patterns. The most useful for a Java project are the end-of-line attributes. Windows editors write CRLF (carriage return and line feed) while Linux and macOS use LF. When contributors on different systems commit the same file with different endings, every line appears changed, diffs are unreadable and shell scripts fail on Linux with errors such as `bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M`. `* text=auto` lets Git normalise text files to LF in the repository; `*.sh text eol=lf` forces LF in the working tree as well (needed for scripts and Dockerfiles that run on Linux); `*.bat text eol=crlf` keeps Windows scripts valid; `*.jar binary` marks binary files so that Git never converts or diffs them as text.

#### Submodules and the alternatives

A **submodule** records another repository's URL in `.gitmodules` and a specific commit of it in the parent's tree (a tree entry of mode `160000`, a "gitlink"). The parent therefore pins an exact version of the child. Clones do not fetch submodule content automatically: `git clone --recurse-submodules` or `git submodule update --init` does. Submodules are suitable for a few vendored repositories that change rarely; they add friction for daily work (detached HEAD inside the submodule, separate commits and pushes, forgotten updates). For Java projects a library published to a Maven repository and declared as a dependency is nearly always the better choice. **Git LFS** (Large File Storage, installed on the build machine as `git-lfs`) is the usual answer for large binary assets: Git stores small pointer files and the content lives on an LFS server.

### Worked example

#### A pre-commit hook that checks Java files

The hook rejects staged Java files that contain tab characters or `System.out.println` calls and compiles the staged files with `javac`. It reads the *staged* content (`git show ":$f"`), not the working tree, so it checks what will be committed.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Reject staged Java files that contain tabs or System.out.println, and run javac on them.
files=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM -- '*.java')
[ -z "$files" ] && exit 0
status=0
for f in $files; do
  if git show ":$f" | grep -q "$(printf '\t')"; then
    echo "pre-commit: tab character in $f (use 4 spaces)"; status=1
  fi
  if git show ":$f" | grep -n 'System\.out\.println'; then
    echo "pre-commit: System.out.println in $f (use a logger)"; status=1
  fi
done
if [ $status -eq 0 ]; then
  out=$(mktemp -d)
  # shellcheck disable=SC2086
  if ! javac -d "$out" $files 2>"$out/err"; then
    echo "pre-commit: compilation failed"; cat "$out/err"; status=1
  fi
  rm -rf "$out"
fi
exit $status
blocks.title: .githooks/pre-commit

blocks.text: The hook was made executable with `chmod +x` and activated with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. It was exercised with a class that violates each rule in turn.

blocks.code:
$ git config core.hooksPath .githooks
$ git add src && git commit -m "Add Greeter"; echo exit=$?
5:        System.out.println("hello");
pre-commit: System.out.println in src/main/java/com/example/orders/Greeter.java (use a logger)
exit=1
$ git add src && git commit -m "Add Greeter"; echo exit=$?
pre-commit: compilation failed
src/main/java/com/example/orders/Greeter.java:5: error: ';' expected
        String s = "hello"
                          ^
1 error
exit=1
$ git add src && git commit -m "Add Greeter"; echo exit=$?
[main (root-commit) a568a7d] Add Greeter
 1 file changed, 7 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 src/main/java/com/example/orders/Greeter.java
exit=0
$ git add src && git commit --no-verify -m "Skip the hook"; echo exit=$?
[main f0bd8f0] Skip the hook
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
exit=0
blocks.title: The hook rejects, then accepts, then is bypassed

blocks.text:
Between the runs the source was edited: the first version printed with `System.out.println`, the second replaced it by a statement with a missing semicolon, the third was valid. The fourth commit reintroduced `System.out.println` and passed only because `--no-verify` skipped the hook, which demonstrates why the server side must enforce the same rules.

#### A commit-msg hook for Conventional Commits

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# Enforce Conventional Commits on the first line of the message.
pattern='^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|ci|build|perf)(\([a-z0-9-]+\))?!?: .{3,}'
if ! head -1 "$1" | grep -Eq "$pattern"; then
  echo "commit-msg: subject must look like 'type(scope): description'"
  exit 1
fi
blocks.title: .githooks/commit-msg

blocks.text:
Git passes the path of the file that holds the message as the first argument. The output of this hook (rejection of `update` `stuff`, acceptance of `docs: describe local setup`) is shown in the chapter on branching strategies.

#### Line endings with .gitattributes

Two files with Windows line endings were committed without attributes. `git ls-files --eol` reports the line-ending state of the index (`i/`) and of the working tree (`w/`).

blocks.code:
$ git ls-files --eol
i/crlf  w/crlf  attr/                   Order.java
i/crlf  w/crlf  attr/                   build.sh
$ cat .gitattributes
*        text=auto
*.java   text eol=lf
*.sh     text eol=lf
*.bat    text eol=crlf
*.jar    binary
$ git add .gitattributes && git commit -m attrs
$ git add --renormalize . ; git status --short
M  Order.java
M  build.sh
$ git ls-files --eol
i/lf    w/lf    attr/text=auto          .gitattributes
i/lf    w/crlf  attr/text eol=lf        Order.java
i/lf    w/crlf  attr/text eol=lf        build.sh
$ git commit -m "Normalize line endings" ; git show --stat --format=%s HEAD | tail -4
 Order.java | 4 ++--
 build.sh   | 4 ++--
 2 files changed, 4 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
blocks.title: Normalising line endings

blocks.text:
Before the attributes both files were stored with CRLF (`i/crlf`). After `git add --renormalize .` the index holds LF (`i/lf`) while the working-tree copies still contain CRLF (`w/crlf`) until they are checked out again (`git rm --cached -r` `. && git reset --hard`, with a clean working tree, or a fresh clone). The normalisation commit changes every line of the affected files once, which is the price of removing the noise permanently.

#### A submodule

blocks.code:
$ git -c protocol.file.allow=always submodule add ../shared-lib libs/shared-lib
Cloning into '/tmp/dvw_v1/work/sub/app/libs/shared-lib'...
done.
$ cat .gitmodules
[submodule "libs/shared-lib"]
        path = libs/shared-lib
        url = ../shared-lib
$ git commit -m "Add shared-lib submodule"
$ git ls-tree HEAD libs/shared-lib
160000 commit c045b43f8c818ca0a7d1da87c840d4e897d2205a  libs/shared-lib
$ git submodule status
 c045b43f8c818ca0a7d1da87c840d4e897d2205a libs/shared-lib (heads/main)
blocks.title: Adding a submodule

blocks.text:
The `-c protocol.file.allow=always` option is needed only because the example clones from a local path; recent Git versions block the `file` transport for submodules by default for security reasons. The tree entry has mode `160000` and type `commit`: the parent stores the id of the child commit, not its files. To advance the pinned version, a developer commits inside the submodule, then commits the new gitlink in the parent.

### Hands-on

1. Enable `core.hooksPath` for `.githooks`, copy the `pre-commit` and `commit-msg` hooks, and confirm that a tab-indented class and the message `wip` are both refused, while `fix(orders): handle null customer` is accepted.
2. Add a `pre-push` hook that runs `mvn -q test` (or any script) and confirm that a failing exit status aborts `git push`; state in one sentence why this is not a substitute for a required status check.
3. Commit two CRLF files, add `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto` and `*.sh text eol=lf`, run `git add` `--renormalize .` and inspect `git ls-files --eol`.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem: line-ending noise hides the real change in a pull request

**Scenario.** A Windows developer edits one line of `OrderService.java`; the pull request shows 400 changed lines. A shell script from the same repository later fails in a Linux container with `bad interpreter`.

**Symptoms.** Every line of the file appears modified; `git diff --ignore-space-at-eol` shows almost nothing; the script fails with `^M` in the interpreter name.

**Diagnosis.** `git ls-files --eol` shows `i/crlf` or mixed endings (listing above). `file build.sh` reports `with CRLF` `line terminators`.

**Root cause.** Different editors and `core.autocrlf` settings convert endings differently, and the repository has no rule.

**Fix.** Commit a `.gitattributes` file with `* text=auto` and explicit `eol=lf` for scripts and Dockerfiles, run `git add` `--renormalize .`, commit the normalisation as a separate commit, and ask collaborators to re-checkout. Add the normalisation commit to `.git-blame-ignore-revs` and `git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs` so that `git blame` skips it (the option name is from memory; verify it).

**Prevention.** Add `.gitattributes` in the first commit and add an editor configuration (`.editorconfig` with `end_of_line = lf`).

#### Problem: the team's hooks do not run on a colleague's machine

**Scenario.** The pre-commit hook works for its author, yet a colleague's commits contain tabs and `System.out.println` calls.

**Symptoms.** Hook failures appear only in continuous integration, never locally.

**Diagnosis.** On the colleague's clone `git config --get core.hooksPath` prints nothing and exits with status 1:

blocks.code:
$ git rev-parse --git-dir; git config --get core.hooksPath; echo "rc=$?"
.git
rc=1
blocks.title: A fresh clone has no hook configuration

blocks.text:
**Root cause.** Hooks and `core.hooksPath` are local; neither is transferred by `git clone`.

**Fix.** Ask the colleague to run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, and provide a one-line setup (a script, or the `exec-maven-plugin` bound to an early lifecycle phase, or a README step).

**Prevention.** Treat hooks as a fast local aid only; enforce the same checks in the pipeline as a required status check, so that a missing hook cannot let a defect into `main`.

### Questions to expect

#### What is a Git hook, and where is it stored?

An executable script with a reserved name (for example `pre-commit`) that Git runs at an event. It is stored in `.git/hooks` or in the directory named by `core.hooksPath`, and it is not versioned or cloned unless the team commits it elsewhere and configures the path.

#### Can hooks be used to enforce team policy?

Not reliably: client-side hooks can be skipped with `--no-verify` or never installed. Policy is enforced on the server with branch protection, required checks and server-side hooks.

#### What does `.gitattributes` do, and why does a Java team need it?

It sets per-path attributes. The common use is line-ending control (`* text=auto`, `eol=lf` for scripts), so that Windows and Linux developers do not produce whole-file diffs and shell scripts keep working in Linux containers.

#### What is a submodule, and what are its drawbacks?

A pinned reference to a specific commit of another repository. Drawbacks: clones need `--recurse-submodules`, updates require two commits, and contributors forget to update. A published Maven artifact is usually preferable.

#### How can a commit be created without running the hooks?

`git commit --no-verify`. This is why important checks are duplicated in the CI pipeline.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Hooks give fast local feedback; they are local, skippable and not cloned, so the same checks must run on the server.

- Share hooks through a committed directory and `core.hooksPath`, set up by each clone.
- `.gitattributes` with `text=auto` and explicit `eol=lf` for scripts prevents line-ending noise.
- Submodules pin another repository's commit; prefer a published library when one exists.
